# ADR 0092 — Repair LamQuant architecture with explicit module ownership and canonical cross-module contracts

> **This file is append-only and living.** Write the decision once. Append dated
> implementation evidence and amendments to the Progress Log. Fill Completion
> and freeze only after every fail-closed gate in this ADR passes.

- **Status:** Proposed 2026-07-09 → Accepted 2026-07-09 → In progress 2026-08-09 → Complete — frozen 2026-08-12
- **Extends:** ADR 0026 (umbrella repository), ADR 0053 (hub/spoke TUI and
  shared config), ADR 0059 (LML ownership), ADR 0066/0068 (measurement and PCCP
  evidence), ADR 0073 (behavioral contracts), ADR 0078 (BLUT typed DAG), and
  ADR 0083 (BLUT interface stack)
- **Scope:** architecture structure only: module ownership, interfaces, seams,
  adapters, dependency direction, test ownership, and executable governance.
  Security hardening and isolated correctness bugs are out of scope unless they
  are direct evidence of a missing or duplicated architectural contract.

## Context

LamQuant has deep domain implementations, but its integration architecture has
not completed the transition from a monolith to a federation of independently
owned repositories. The repository describes standalone modules and pinned
gitlinks while required code still arrives through ignored directories and
sibling paths. Shared TUI, config, execution, artifact, protocol, and evaluation
concepts have more than one implementation or more than one interpretation.
Root tests and ADR views still encode parts of the previous repository shape.

This is not a decision to rewrite working domain cores. The executor facade,
LMA archive facade, lossless codec kernels, and other modules pass the deletion
test: removing them would spread complexity across callers. The required work
is to deepen those modules, move seams to real variation points, and remove
parallel implementations that dilute locality.

The audit found one systemic risk: **local correctness can coexist with global
incoherence**. A caller can compile against a sibling path, a TUI can invoke a
different command than the CLI, a cache can return a path that exists only on
the producing host, or a generated ADR view can disagree with prose. Each case
is locally plausible because no canonical module owns the complete contract.

## Evidence Baseline

- Architecture audit source snapshot: root commit `ce251194`; numbering and ADR
  write started from root commit `f8e9745a` on 2026-07-09.
- Audit covered root manifests and tools plus the lossless, neural, evaluation,
  firmware, training, TUI, operations, visualization, and ADR modules.
- The worktree contained concurrent submodule and generated-document changes.
  Findings below were included only when independently visible in tracked source;
  dirty benchmark/proposal output was not treated as architecture evidence.
- Root `cargo check --workspace --all-targets` passed during the audit, while
  root `cargo test --workspace` exposed stale TUI expectations and root pytest
  collection failed on removed monolith imports. These are symptoms of contract
  drift, not the sole basis for this decision.
- `tests/codec/test_l5_cross_lang.py` was byte-identical to its owner copy under
  `codec-lossless/tests/codec/`, proving at least one live mirrored test. This ADR
  does not depend on an unverified repository-wide duplicate count.

## Decision

LamQuant will run one ordered architecture-stabilization campaign. Every
cross-module concept will have one canonical owner module and one tested
interface. Repository manifests and gitlinks will describe the dependency graph
that a clean checkout actually builds. Adapters will exist only at real process,
network, storage, platform, format, or execution seams. Root tests will verify
public contracts; implementation tests will live with their owner. Existing deep
facades will be preserved and deepened rather than split into pass-through
modules. The eighteen remediation items below are mandatory; no item may be
closed by documentation alone or by a waived, skipped, or unmeasured gate.

This ADR fixes seam placement and ownership. It deliberately does **not** freeze
detailed Rust/Python/TypeScript interfaces. Each implementation phase may design
its smallest viable interface, but that design must satisfy the invariants and
gates recorded here. A hard-to-reverse interface choice may receive a focused
follow-up ADR; such an ADR extends this campaign and cannot weaken its gates.

## Architectural Invariants

1. **Executable module graph.** Every required module is tracked or published,
   version-pinned, and buildable from a clean recursive checkout. Ignored or
   undeclared sibling code cannot be a production dependency.
2. **One canonical owner.** Persistence policy, execution lifecycle, artifact
   identity, wire protocol, format parsing, and promotion semantics each have
   one owner module. Callers cannot reimplement owner policy.
3. **Real seams only.** A seam needs real variation. One production adapter with
   no second real or test adapter stays private to its implementation. An
   editable-development path override is build-time dependency selection, not a
   published interface, so it does not create a public adapter seam.
4. **One application execution path.** CLI, TUI, local execution, and remote
   execution resolve operations through the same application-level module.
5. **Interface is test surface.** Owner-local tests exercise implementation;
   root tests exercise binaries, protocols, artifacts, and other public
   interfaces. Root tests do not import carved implementation packages.
6. **Portable content identity.** Invocation identity and content identity are
   distinct. Cached artifacts own or can rehydrate their bytes and metadata on
   another host after the producer job directory is removed.
7. **Preserve earned depth.** Large files are not split merely by line count.
   Deep facades remain stable while private implementation absorbs duplication.
8. **Machine-readable governance.** ADR lifecycle, supersession, topology, and
   generated views derive from validated metadata and source manifests.
9. **Replace, do not layer.** A canonical implementation replaces duplicate
   implementations in the same phase. Compatibility adapters must be temporary,
   named, tested, and removed by that phase's gate.
10. **Fail closed.** Missing dependencies, unknown lifecycle states, skipped
    contract tests, missing measurements, and unclassified findings fail gates.

## Problem Inventory and Mandated Remediation

### A01 — Repository graph claims isolation that source does not provide

- **Problem and evidence:** `.gitignore` hides `training/backends`, yet the
  LamQuant, Lamu, and core cookbooks require it by path. It is neither tracked as
  a gitlink nor backed by a configured remote. `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` claims
  standalone git-revision seams, while lossless, firmware, visualization, and
  Eagle manifests depend on sibling paths. Root Cargo metadata covers only a
  subset of the declared repository graph.
- **Mandated fix:** track and pin every required repository or publish its owned
  interface artifact. Move any implementation with no independent owner into
  its real owner. Permit sibling path overrides only as an explicit editable-dev
  adapter; never as the clean-build dependency. Generate topology views from
  `.gitmodules` and package manifests.
- **Owner and dependency:** meta-repository; first dependency for all later work.
- **Gate:** a temporary clean recursive clone builds every declared owner
  workspace with network-independent pins and no ignored/untracked dependency;
  `python3 tools/architecture_gate.py --finding A01` exits `0`.

### A02 — Root tests retain monolith ownership and mirror owner tests

- **Problem and evidence:** `tests/conftest.py` acknowledges removed root
  implementations, but root tests still import `ai_models`, training internals,
  and other carved packages. Root `pyproject.toml` configures pytest but does not
  install an integration package. Collection fails before tests run, and at
  least one lossless test is byte-identical at root and in its owner repository.
- **Mandated fix:** move all implementation tests to owner repositories. Delete
  root mirrors. Keep only contract and conformance tests at root, crossing public
  binaries, protocols, schemas, wire vectors, and artifacts. One declarative test
  taxonomy drives pytest markers, local runners, and CI.
- **Owner and dependency:** meta-repository owns root conformance tests; each
  domain repository owns its relocated implementation tests. Depends on A01's
  truthful module graph.
- **Gate:** `pytest -q tests/contracts` exits `0`; root collection imports no
  implementation-only package; owner-local CI runs every rehomed test;
  `python3 tools/architecture_gate.py --finding A02` exits `0`.

### A03 — ADR lifecycle and relationship truth are split across prose and metadata

- **Problem and evidence:** template/body lifecycle vocabulary differs from
  frontmatter vocabulary and `tools/doc_views.py`. Frozen prose can coexist with
  `accepted` frontmatter; ADR 0082 lacks a classified status; ADR 0072 references
  the wrong predecessor; ADRs 0079/0080 declare supersession in prose but not
  metadata. Mutable ledgers are also stored as ADRs despite the one-unit-of-work
  rule.
- **Mandated fix:** create one ADR governance module that validates required
  sections, lifecycle transitions, references, reciprocal supersession, and
  freeze immutability. Generate body status displays and cross-cutting views from
  canonical metadata. Move mutable execution ledgers and backlogs outside the
  ADR directory, leaving links from decisions.
- **Owner and dependency:** meta-repository documentation tooling; may proceed
  with A01; both must land before Phase 2 may start.
- **Gate:** `python3 tools/adr_lint.py --strict`,
  `python3 tools/doc_tree_lint.py --strict`, and `python3 tools/doc_views.py`
  all exit `0`; no ADR is unclassified and every relationship resolves.

### A04 — Bootstrap mixes reproducible-build and editable-development states

- **Problem and evidence:** `tools/bootstrap.sh` changes into `tools/` before
  writing `env.sh`, so paths resolve under the wrong root. Bootstrap preserves
  detached pins while checkout/merge hooks attach branches, and hook branch
  lookup uses keys that do not match `.gitmodules` section names. Architecture
  documentation describes a different topology and branch policy.
- **Mandated fix:** expose explicit pinned-build and editable-development
  adapters behind one bootstrap module. Pinned mode never changes gitlinks;
  editable mode attaches only configured branches/worktrees. Both derive paths
  from a computed repository root and consume generated topology.
- **Owner and dependency:** meta-repository; depends on A01's canonical graph.
- **Gate:** clean temporary clones pass `tools/bootstrap.sh --build --check` and
  `tools/bootstrap.sh --dev --check`; repeated runs are idempotent; generated
  environment paths point to repository-root locations.

### A05 — Spoke execution is reconstructed by each caller

- **Problem and evidence:** umbrella CLI delegation drops the operation token;
  TUI codec execution calls a runner that uses `current_exe()` and therefore can
  respawn the hub; SSH command construction prepends an operation to arguments
  that already contain the full command. Launcher descriptors also hard-code
  repository layout in the operations module.
- **Mandated fix:** one deep spoke-execution module owns operation resolution,
  executable selection, argument construction, process lifecycle, structured
  outcomes, and component-owned launch descriptors. CLI and TUI are callers;
  local process and SSH execution are adapters.
- **Owner and dependency:** `lamquant-ops`; depends on A01 and constrains A06.
- **Gate:** one table-driven contract suite runs every supported operation
  through direct CLI, hub CLI, TUI request, local adapter, and SSH command
  rendering and proves equivalent operation identity and terminal outcome.

### A06 — Shared TUI module remains forked rather than deep

- **Problem and evidence:** shared and hub `App` implementations remain roughly
  2.3k and 3.0k lines, while copied output/settings panels differ mainly in
  branding and hub descriptors. ADR 0053 calls for a generic shared App and thin
  spoke/hub adapters, but navigation, event handling, and state still fork.
- **Mandated fix:** one shared TUI module owns event loop, navigation, state
  transitions, and common panels. Routes, domain actions, settings descriptors,
  and branding enter through narrow inputs. Delete copied panels and the hub's
  direct full-spoke dependency.
- **Owner and dependency:** `lamquant-tui`; depends on A05 for operation actions.
- **Gate:** hub and spoke golden/state-transition tests run through one shared
  harness; a duplicate-implementation guard finds no second App/event loop or
  copied common panel; hub dependency graph contains no full codec spoke.

### A07 — TUI bypasses canonical config ownership

- **Problem and evidence:** `lamquant-tui` declares `lamquant-config` but does not
  use it. TUI config code owns path selection, loading, saving, and a hand-written
  TOML parser while the canonical config module already owns load recovery and
  atomic save. Runtime application is attached to a value object through an
  empty method.
- **Mandated fix:** canonical config module owns persisted values, parsing,
  recovery, migration, and atomic save. TUI maps view state only. Runtime changes
  cross an injected capability adapter, separate from the persisted value.
- **Owner and dependency:** `lamquant-config` with `lamquant-tui` adapter; may
  proceed with A06 after shared state responsibilities are named.
- **Gate:** config corruption/recovery, atomic-write failure, CLI/TUI parity, and
  runtime-effect tests cross canonical config and capability interfaces; no TUI
  source implements an independent parser or save path.

### A08 — Training execution modes have incompatible lifecycles

- **Problem and evidence:** local `run_node` owns typed failures, retries,
  cancellation, and soft/hard timeouts. Standalone P2P and cloud CLI paths
  transport artifacts, but executor-integrated P2P does not: `DispatchRequest`
  carries neither artifact nor source root, the coordinator sends
  `encrypted_input: None`, the peer rejects it, and successful output cannot
  return through `DispatchHandle`. Remote failures flatten to strings; cloud
  uses a separate lifecycle and is not an executor adapter. Remote polling does
  not observe plan cancellation or wall-clock deadline, coordinator cancellation
  does not signal assigned work, and disconnect/lease terminal rules differ.
- **Mandated fix:** preserve the executor facade and place one execution
  lifecycle/state-machine implementation behind it. Local, P2P, and cloud are
  adapters that share serializable outcomes, wall-clock deadlines, cancellation,
  assignment ownership, and terminal-state rules.
- **Owner and dependency:** BLUT training engine; depends directly on A09's
  artifact identity. Completion also waits for A10 because remote adapters reach
  object storage through the artifact module rather than owning storage policy.
- **Gate:** the same lifecycle contract suite passes for local, P2P, and cloud
  adapters. It covers cancellation while queued, assigned, running, polling,
  uploading, and downloading; hanging submit/poll/transfer/stage; peer disconnect;
  lease expiry and fenced retry; typed failure identity; artifact round-trip; and
  exactly one terminal outcome. No adapter reports success without validated
  artifact identity and rehydrated output.

### A09 — Cache stores nonportable handles and conflates two identities

- **Problem and evidence:** cache entries and their remote tier serialize
  `ErasedArtifact` handles while payload bytes remain under producer job paths.
  The P2P bundle path can rehydrate bytes, but cache lookup does not use that
  capability. Cross-host hits and deleted job directories therefore return stale
  paths. Invocation keys are reused as expected output or lineage hashes even
  though bundle code hashes produced bytes separately.
- **Mandated fix:** preserve existing content-hash derivation, but represent
  invocation key and content identity as distinct types. One content-addressed
  artifact module owns canonical payload, metadata, validation, and consumer-local
  rehydration. Invocation cache maps invocation identity to content identity;
  cache values retain no producer-local path; lineage consumes content identity
  only. Expected remote output identity is supplied only when analytically known;
  otherwise the worker returns identity and the receiver independently recomputes
  it. Cache lookup validates the artifact contract before returning a hit.
- **Owner and dependency:** BLUT training engine; follows A01 and supplies the
  artifact contract consumed by A10 and A08.
- **Gate:** produce path-bearing file and directory artifacts on host A, populate
  shared cache, delete A's job directory, then consume on host B with byte-identical
  validated content and B-local paths. Missing or modified payload never produces
  a hit. Cold `StageEnd` and warm `StageSkipped` lineage hashes match. Invocation
  key and content identity differ for a nontrivial stage, and type checking prevents
  passing one where the other is required.

### A10 — Two object-store modules own divergent policy

- **Problem and evidence:** asynchronous cloud storage and synchronous framework
  storage define separate `BlobStore` interfaces with different size limits and
  error behavior for the same external dependency.
- **Mandated fix:** one object-storage policy module owns typed key namespaces,
  addressing, maximum sizes, hash verification, not-found semantics, error
  taxonomy, idempotent writes, and production adapters. Async production access
  is canonical; blocking callers cross one explicit adapter rather than defining
  another storage policy interface.
- **Owner and dependency:** BLUT training engine; follows A09 so artifact policy
  determines storage requirements.
- **Gate:** one conformance suite runs against filesystem and production
  object-store adapters through async and blocking access where both remain. It
  proves identical not-found, oversize, wrong-hash, corruption, idempotent-put,
  concurrent-put, and byte-round-trip behavior. Cache and cloud consume one
  canonical storage policy interface.

### A11 — Lossless CLI interleaves schema, workflows, I/O, and rendering

- **Problem and evidence:** `lamquant-lossless/src/bin/lml.rs` is approximately
  10.8k lines and combines command schema, routing, filesystem/network actions,
  wire parsing, progress, rendering, exit policy, and domain workflows. Archive
  verification has separate compact and explain procedures.
- **Mandated fix:** preserve command names and serialized CLI behavior while
  moving codec, archive, and verification workflows behind result-producing
  modules. Clap parsing, progress, stdout/stderr rendering, and exit mapping stay
  in a thin CLI adapter. Do not create one shallow module per command.
- **Owner and dependency:** lossless repository; depends on A01 and coordinates
  with A12/A14.
- **Gate:** workflow tests require no process/stdout capture; compact, explain,
  JSON, and TUI render the same structured verification result; CLI smoke/golden
  tests prove command compatibility.

### A12 — LMA facade leaks archive layout and verification mechanics

- **Problem and evidence:** LMA callers choose among unrelated list, extract,
  append, unpack, mmap, raw/header/decoded read, and manifest paths while learning
  v1/v2 offsets, decoding, hashing, and tempfile behavior. CLI verification
  re-learns archive layout in two implementations.
- **Mandated fix:** retain one LMA archive facade and deepen it. Version parsing,
  buffered/mmap access, reconstruction, hashing, temporary storage, and structured
  verification become private implementation or internal adapters. Renderers
  consume one verification result.
- **Owner and dependency:** lossless archive module; supplies A11 workflows.
- **Gate:** one archive conformance matrix passes across v1/v2, buffered/mmap,
  list/read/extract/append/unpack/verify, corruption, and round-trip cases; CLI
  contains no archive-layout parsing.

### A13 — MCU/Desktop seam exposes codec implementation details

- **Problem and evidence:** MCU exports broad hidden preparation, per-channel,
  decode-plan, synthesis, and finalization functions solely for Desktop. Desktop
  orchestrates these details and re-exports the MCU crate, so kernel refactors
  cross the crate seam.
- **Mandated fix:** no-std codec owns end-to-end packet orchestration behind its
  small external codec interface. Serial and Rayon implementations become two
  internal execution adapters. Host file/stdin/network/container I/O stays in
  the host owner, not the firmware-floor module.
- **Owner and dependency:** lossless MCU core and Desktop adapter; independent of
  A11 except for final public workflow integration.
- **Gate:** existing byte-equal backend tests plus serial/Rayon decode parity pass
  for all golden vectors; Desktop imports no preparation or decode-plan internals;
  MCU public surface contains no host `Read`/`Write` convenience policy.

### A14 — Container parsing is duplicated by format and access mode

- **Problem and evidence:** ABIR/BCS1 wire parsing, whole-buffer decode policy,
  streaming index/footer behavior, and frozen legacy streaming code overlap.
  Streaming explicitly copies footer logic, while a delegating reader repeats
  dispatch boilerplate.
- **Mandated fix:** legacy and BCS1 format adapters normalize version-specific
  headers into one internal container plan. One deep reader implementation owns
  metadata, indexing, footer/framing behavior, codec dispatch, and seeking across
  memory and file sources.
- **Owner and dependency:** lossless container module; supplies A11 and may share
  verification results with A12.
- **Gate:** one reader conformance suite passes every supported format against
  memory/file and whole-buffer/streaming sources, including indexed seek and
  truncated/corrupt input; copied footer/parser implementation is deleted.

### A15 — Firmware stages exist without one typed end-to-end pipeline

- **Problem and evidence:** target loops leave ADC input unwired; SNN initialization
  is not part of pipeline boot; scheduler output and FSQ input use incompatible
  maps/shapes; encode results are discarded rather than transported. Acquisition,
  inference, encoding, and transport therefore have no shared ownership law.
- **Mandated fix:** one firmware pipeline module owns boot state, complete-window
  ownership, acquisition → inference → encoding → transport progression, and
  terminal outcome. ADC/DMA and transport are platform adapters. The SNN-to-FSQ
  transformation is explicit and typed inside the pipeline.
- **Owner and dependency:** firmware common module plus target adapters; extends
  ADR 0073 and coordinates with A16.
- **Gate:** a host pipeline harness and target build tests prove one acquired
  window initializes inference, produces the expected typed map, encodes once,
  and reaches a transport sink; missing stage readiness cannot enter Operational.

### A16 — Firmware, GUI, and Tauri use different protocol contracts

- **Problem and evidence:** firmware contains a dormant Postcard envelope and a
  separate `LAMR` USB frame; GUI serial parsing expects a custom `0xAA` packet;
  TypeScript and Rust disagree on at least one Tauri command's arguments and
  return type.
- **Mandated fix:** one versioned wire-types/protocol module owns frame identity,
  versioning, payload types, and structured outcomes. Firmware, serial/native GUI,
  and Tauri are adapters. Generate TypeScript bindings or schema from canonical
  types and keep firmware-host golden vectors.
- **Owner and dependency:** `lamquant-ipc-types` owns versioned firmware/host
  envelopes and payload types; firmware and visualization provide adapters.
  Depends on A15 data shape.
- **Gate:** firmware ↔ host golden vectors and Rust ↔ TypeScript command contract
  tests pass; unsupported versions fail; generated bindings are current; no
  independent frame constant or command-shape definition remains in adapters.

### A17 — Evaluation mixes measurement, decision, promotion, and recording

- **Problem and evidence:** neural PCCP gate code combines evaluator process
  execution, path discovery, metric parsing, criterion semantics, promotion,
  capture, and verdict persistence. Evaluator paths still reference the old
  repository layout. Eagle resolves a crates.io OpenECS version different from
  the local standard implementation.
- **Mandated fix:** evaluator adapters produce finite, versioned, provenanced
  measurements. One promotion-decision module applies criteria. A separate
  recorder persists the outcome. Pin one OpenECS/LQS standard source and version
  across evaluation consumers.
- **Owner and dependency:** `codec-neural` PCCP decision module owns promotion
  policy and verdict recording; OpenECS owns the measurement standard. Evaluator
  adapters consume both. Depends on A01's source graph and A02's test ownership.
- **Gate:** typed measurement contract tests cover missing/non-finite values and
  evaluator process failure; decision tests require complete provenance; recorder
  round-trips outcomes; all consumers resolve the same OpenECS/LQS source/version.

### A18 — Transport interface is hypothetical with one adapter

- **Problem and evidence:** `lamquant-ops` exposes a general transport interface,
  but SSH is its only real adapter. The interface adds public surface before
  demonstrating varying behavior.
- **Mandated fix:** decide during A05. If a second real adapter is required, prove
  variance with shared contract tests. Otherwise keep transport private inside
  spoke-execution implementation and remove the public seam. Do not preserve the
  interface solely to support mocks.
- **Owner and dependency:** `lamquant-ops`; final cleanup of A05.
- **Gate:** architecture gate observes either two real adapters passing one
  contract suite or no public transport interface. A one-adapter public seam
  fails.

## Target Module Graph

```text
tracked/pinned owner repositories
        |
        +-- root conformance tests (public contracts only)
        |
        +-- CLI/TUI --> spoke-execution --> local | SSH adapters
        |                 |
        |                 +-- shared TUI --> canonical config --> runtime adapter
        |
        +-- training executor facade --> execution lifecycle
        |                               --> local | P2P | cloud adapters
        |                               --> artifact store --> object storage
        |
        +-- lossless workflows --> codec core --> serial | Rayon adapters
        |                     --> container reader --> legacy | BCS1 adapters
        |                     --> LMA archive --> buffered | mmap internals
        |
        +-- firmware pipeline --> ADC/DMA | transport adapters
        |                     --> versioned protocol <-- GUI/Tauri adapters
        |
        +-- evaluator adapters --> typed measurement --> promotion decision
                                                     --> verdict recorder
```

This graph shows ownership, not a mandate for one crate per box. A module may be
a crate, package, or private tier-spanning slice. Implementations may contain
private internal seams; only caller-visible variation belongs in external
interfaces.

## Dependency Order and Phases

1. **Phase 0 — Gate scaffold:** add `tools/architecture_gate.py`, finding IDs,
   clean-clone harness, and machine-readable gate report. A03 adds the missing
   `tools/adr_lint.py`; existing doc-tree, compose, and view tools remain inputs
   to the completion gate. Baseline failures must be recorded; the scaffold
   cannot classify a missing test as pass.
2. **Phase 1 — Foundation:** A01–A04. No cross-repository refactor starts until
   A01 establishes truthful source ownership. A02/A03/A04 may then proceed in
   parallel.
3. **Phase 2 — Operations shell:** A05 and A07 may proceed in parallel; A06 then
   composes canonical operation actions and config ownership into one shared TUI.
4. **Phase 3 — Training:** A09, then A10, then A08. Artifact identity names
   payloads; object storage implements artifact policy; lifecycle carries those
   artifacts and outcomes across local, P2P, and cloud adapters.
5. **Phase 4 — Lossless:** A13 and A14 may begin in parallel; A12 deepens archive
   ownership; A11 finishes by composing those modules behind stable CLI behavior.
6. **Phase 5 — Edge/evaluation:** A15 precedes A16's final data shape. A17 depends
   only on A01/A02 and may start as soon as Phase 1 completes; it is grouped here
   because its outputs join the edge/evaluation completion evidence.
7. **Phase 6 — Seam cleanup:** A18 and repository-wide duplicate/dependency
   guards. Remove all temporary compatibility adapters before completion.

Phases 3, 4, and 5 may run in parallel after Phase 1 and their named dependencies
pass. Each phase must be independently reviewable and revertible. This ADR does
not authorize one repository-wide implementation commit.

## Rationale

- Truthful source ownership is first because every later seam depends on knowing
  which repository can change and test the implementation.
- One canonical owner creates locality: fixes, invariants, and verification
  concentrate instead of spreading across callers.
- Deep modules create leverage: CLI/TUI, local/remote, serial/parallel, and
  firmware/GUI callers reuse behavior through small interfaces.
- Public contracts are the correct root test surface. Importing owner internals
  from root rebuilds the monolith through tests even if source repositories are
  separate.
- Preserving executor, archive, and codec facades avoids file-size refactoring
  that merely moves complexity. Their internal implementations should absorb
  duplicated policy.
- Content-addressed, rehydratable artifacts are required by the already-chosen
  local/P2P/cloud execution model. Path-bearing handles cannot satisfy that model.
- Machine-readable ADR and topology governance prevents architecture prose from
  becoming a second, weaker source of truth.
- Dependency-ordered phases reduce risk and allow parallel work only after
  foundational contracts are executable.

## Alternatives Considered

- **Return to one monolithic repository/workspace.** Rejected. It would hide
  ownership leaks by making sibling paths legal, not establish durable module
  interfaces. Independent firmware, training, evaluation, and codec ownership
  remains useful.
- **Patch each observed bug without changing ownership.** Rejected. Delegation,
  cache, protocol, and test failures recur because several callers own the same
  policy. Local fixes would preserve the cause.
- **Split every large file into smaller files.** Rejected. Line count does not
  measure depth. Splitting executor or LMA public behavior into pass-through
  modules would enlarge interfaces and reduce locality.
- **Rewrite integration modules from scratch.** Rejected. Existing facades,
  tests, formats, and command behavior carry compatibility value. Replace
  duplicate implementations behind stable behavior in narrow phases.
- **Keep all eighteen items as an informal backlog.** Rejected. Existing ADR and
  topology drift proves prose without fail-closed gates does not constrain work.
- **Create eighteen ADRs immediately.** Rejected for this decision. Seam
  placement, dependency order, and completion criteria form one stabilization
  campaign. Focused follow-up ADRs are reserved for hard-to-reverse interface
  trade-offs discovered during implementation, not routine execution tasks.
- **Preserve every abstraction for test mocking.** Rejected. One adapter is a
  hypothetical seam. Tests should cross the same real interface as callers or
  use private internal seams owned by the module.

## Consequences

### Positive

- Clean checkouts become sufficient to build and test every declared module.
- One fix applies across all callers of execution, config, artifact, protocol,
  archive, container, and evaluation modules.
- Root integration tests become smaller and more stable because they stop
  importing implementation details.
- Domain repositories can evolve privately behind conformance-tested interfaces.
- Architecture diagrams, ADR views, and CI derive from executable truth.

### Costs and constraints

- Some repositories or packages must be published, tracked, moved, or deleted.
- Root test count will fall while owner-local test count and contract-test quality
  rise; raw root test count cannot be used as progress evidence.
- Temporary compatibility adapters may be necessary, but each must have a named
  removal gate in the same phase.
- CLI/TUI and protocol refactors require golden compatibility fixtures before
  moving implementation.
- Training artifact migration needs explicit handling for old cache entries;
  silently treating path handles as portable is forbidden.
- Generated documentation will change when canonical ADR metadata is repaired.
- Completion requires all owner workspaces, not only the root Cargo workspace,
  to pass their gates.

  `architecture_gate.py` must invoke its owner-local suite, encode the behavioral

- **Completion gate (fail-CLOSED; unmeasured ⇒ FAIL):**

  ```sh
  python3 tools/architecture_gate.py --strict && \
  python3 tools/adr_lint.py --strict && \
  python3 tools/doc_tree_lint.py --strict && \
  python3 tools/doc_compose.py && \

  cargo fmt --all -- --check && \
  cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings && \
  cargo test --workspace --all-targets && \
  pytest -q tests/contracts
  ```

- **Pass when:** all commands exit `0`; architecture gate reports A01–A18

  subgate builds every owner workspace from pinned/tracked inputs; generated
  views are current; owner-local CI evidence is attached to the gate report.
- **Rollback:** revert each implementation phase independently and append the
  failed gate evidence here. Preserve architecture finding IDs, contract tests,
  and gate infrastructure unless a superseding ADR names an equivalent
  replacement. Never restore a duplicate implementation merely to keep a new
  interface alive.

# ADR 0093: Ship a `blut-web` sidecar (axum + Leptos/WASM) that serves a read-only dashboard v1 over status.jsonl and escalates to live control v2 through the CLI exec-bridge, keeping the engine HTTP-free

<!-- The title IS this ADR's one-line summary in the generated index/digest. -->

> **This file is append-only and living.** Write the decision once. As
> implementation proceeds, **append** dated entries to the Progress Log — never
> rewrite or delete earlier text; correct an earlier statement with a *new* dated
> entry beneath it, so the original stays as historical record. When the
> deliverable passes its gate, fill **Completion** and set Status to
> `Complete — frozen YYYY-MM-DD`. A frozen ADR is permanent. To reverse a frozen
> decision later, write a *new* ADR that supersedes it (updating this one's
> Status pointer is the only edit allowed after freeze).

## Status

`Proposed 2026-07-10` → `In progress` → `Complete — frozen 2026-07-19`

## Context

Every premier orchestrator has a web UI: Dagit/Dagster UI, FlyteConsole, the
Prefect UI, Argo's workflow UI. It is the surface a team actually watches — DAG
run state, resource pressure, retries, lineage — and the one competitors are
judged on in a bake-off. BLUT has a strong TUI (the console + DAG builder shipped
this session, `src/tui/`) but zero browser presence, which caps it at
single-operator, single-terminal use and makes it invisible to anyone who
evaluates orchestrators through a dashboard.

The constraint is ADR 0034 / ADR 0083: the engine (`blut/src`) must stay
HTTP-free — no axum, no server, no webhook listener linked into the engine
binary. ADR 0083 already reserves `blut-web` as a sidecar crate and names the
building blocks: `blut-types` (wasm32-safe serde wire types shared with the TUI),
`include_dir!`-embedded Leptos bundle, and the exec-bridge pattern for any
mutation. This ADR commits to actually building that surface and fixes its v1/v2
scope.

## Decision

BLUT will build `crates/blut-web`, a standalone sidecar binary (dispatched as
`blut web`, ADR 0083 external-subcommand pattern) that hosts an axum server and
serves a Leptos+WASM single-page dashboard embedded via `include_dir!`. It shares
all wire types with the TUI through `blut-types` — the front-end deserializes the
exact same `StageEvent`/`HostedEvent`/PlanSpec/lineage rows the console renders,
so there is one schema, not two. **v1 is strictly read-only:** the server tails
`status.jsonl`, the lineage SQLite, the PeerRegistry (mesh, ADR 0079), the
PrivacyLedger (ε, ADR 0080), the broker envelope (ADR 0046/0047), and the plan
registry (ADR 0085), and pushes updates to the browser over SSE; it opens no
write path into the engine and holds no engine state. **v2 adds live control
only through the exec-bridge** (ADR 0083): a mutating action (run, cancel,
promote, rollback) shells out to the CLI (`blut run … via systemd-run --user`,
`blut cancel`, `blut plan promote`) — the same enforcement path a human uses — so
there is never a second way to mutate the system and never engine-internal
mutation from HTTP. Every control action is gated by RBAC (ADR 0095) and written
to the audit log before dispatch. The engine remains HTTP-free: `blut-web` links
`blut-types` but never the engine lib; it reads the engine's artifacts, it does
not embed the engine. Clinical/PHI stays behind the hard-block (ADR 0061) — a
`restricted` tenant's status/lineage is never served to a shared-tenant web
session, and the sidecar refuses to render Restricted artifacts off-box.

## Rationale

- Read-only-first is the honest MVP: 90% of a dashboard's value (see it, don't
  fly blind) needs zero write path and zero new trust surface — it is pure
  consumption of artifacts that already exist and are already the TUI's inputs.
- Sharing `blut-types` means the web and TUI cannot drift; a schema change breaks
  both compiles at once (the wasm32 CI check on `blut-types`, ADR 0083, keeps the
  browser build honest).
- The exec-bridge gives one enforcement path for humans and API — retries, broker
  admission (ADR 0046, never bypassed), audit logging, and clinical gating all
  live in the CLI, so the web surface inherits them instead of re-implementing
  (and diverging).
- `include_dir!` + one binary = zero deploy steps (no separate static host, no
  CDN), matching the "operator opts into a sidecar, systemd supervises it"
  model.
- Keeping axum out of the engine preserves the lean-CLI, offline-capable,
  MCU-adjacent posture the charter protects (ADR 0034).

## Alternatives Considered

- **Put the axum server in the engine behind a `web` feature flag.** Rejected:
  ADR 0034 bans an in-engine HTTP server outright, and a feature flag does not
  change that a server compiled into `blut` can be linked, shipped, and left
  listening — the boundary is the source tree, not a cargo flag (ADR 0083). It
  would also drag axum/tokio-http into the dependency tree the lean-CLI story
  depends on staying small.
- **A JS/TS front-end (React) talking to a thin Rust JSON API.** Rejected: it
  breaks the locked "web = Leptos + WASM, Rust end-to-end" decision (ADR 0083)
  and forces a *second* type definition of the wire schema in TypeScript, which
  is exactly the drift `blut-types` exists to prevent — a bake-off dashboard that
  disagrees with the TUI about run state is worse than none.
- **Let the web sidecar mutate engine state directly via a shared IPC socket.**
  Rejected: a direct mutation path means two enforcement routes (human CLI vs web
  IPC) that will drift on retry/broker/audit/clinical semantics; the exec-bridge
  deliberately funnels both through the CLI so broker admission (ADR 0046) and the
  clinical block (ADR 0061) cannot be bypassed by the web door.

## Consequences

- Upside: BLUT becomes multi-viewer and browser-visible without the engine
  growing a server; it is now legible in an orchestrator bake-off.
- Upside: the plan registry (ADR 0085), mesh (0079), ε-ledger (0080), and broker
  (0046) all get a first-class visual surface for free — they already emit the
  artifacts the dashboard reads.
- Downside: a second front-end to keep in lockstep with the TUI (mitigated by
  `blut-types`, but Leptos component work is real UI cost); an SSE fan-out server
  to operate and secure.
- Downside: v2's exec-bridge inherits `systemd-run --user` as the dispatch
  substrate, so the web control plane only works where that exists (not bare
  containers without a user bus) — a documented deploy constraint.
- Constraint locked: no mutating web endpoint may ever reach engine internals;
  the day one does, the two-enforcement-path drift this ADR forbids has begun.

## Implementation Plan  *(the contract — write once; amend only by a dated Progress Log entry)*

- **Deliverable:** `crates/blut-web` — an axum sidecar serving an
  `include_dir!`-embedded Leptos+WASM dashboard that renders live DAG / mesh /
  cache / ε / broker / registry state from `status.jsonl` + the lineage DB over
  SSE (v1 read-only); v2 adds exec-bridge control actions gated by ADR 0095.
- **Acceptance gate (fail-CLOSED; unmeasured ⇒ FAIL):**
  - `gate_cmd:` `cargo test -p blut-web --test dashboard_readonly` — boots the
    sidecar against a fixture `status.jsonl`, asserts the SSE stream reflects a
    node state transition, asserts `GET`/`POST` to every route is side-effect-free
    on the engine (no engine mutation path exists), and asserts a `restricted`
    fixture is not served.
  - `pass when:` `exit == 0` — the dashboard reflects the fixture run, and a
    grep of the crate for a direct engine-state write returns nothing (mutation
    only via `std::process::Command` to the CLI).
- **Rollback:** `blut-web` is an opt-in sidecar; not building/running it removes
  the entire web surface with zero engine impact — the TUI remains the control
  plane.

## Progress Log  *(append-only; newest last; never rewrite an earlier entry)*

- _2026-07-10 — opened._
- _2026-07-19 — v1 (read-only) COMPLETE; ADR frozen._ The sidecar shipped its
  read surface in ADR 0083 M2 (jobs / status / lineage graph+card+diff / model
  pointers as JSON, `blut-types` wire types shared with the TUI, embedded
  Leptos dashboard, custody fail-closed). This increment adds the last v1
  piece — **SSE live-tail** (`GET /api/jobs/{id}/events`): status.jsonl IS the
  bus; the endpoint re-reads it every 300ms and emits each newly-appended
  *complete* line as a `text/event-stream` `data:` frame, resetting cleanly on
  rotation, opening no write path into the engine (the client dropping the
  connection drops the stream). **v2 live control** (the ADR's escalation) also
  already landed in M2 as the exec bridge (`POST /api/jobs` run, `POST
  /api/jobs/{id}/cancel`) — `rbac::enforce` (Operator floor, allow+deny audited

# ADR 0094: Turn BLUT's sensor substrate into an event/data-driven trigger system — a file/spool/cron sensor daemon, sidecar webhook ingress, a `blut-notify` sink crate, and declarative SLA rules

<!-- The title IS this ADR's one-line summary in the generated index/digest. -->

> **This file is append-only and living.** Write the decision once. As
> implementation proceeds, **append** dated entries to the Progress Log — never
> rewrite or delete earlier text; correct an earlier statement with a *new* dated
> entry beneath it, so the original stays as historical record. When the
> deliverable passes its gate, fill **Completion** and set Status to
> `Complete — frozen YYYY-MM-DD`. A frozen ADR is permanent. To reverse a frozen
> decision later, write a *new* ADR that supersedes it (updating this one's
> Status pointer is the only edit allowed after freeze).

## Status

`Proposed 2026-07-10` → `In progress` → `Complete — frozen 2026-07-19`

## Context

Airflow and Prefect sensors, plus their alerting integrations, let a pipeline be
*triggered by the world* (a file lands, an S3 prefix fills, a cron fires, a
webhook arrives) and let operators be *notified* when a run breaks or overruns.
This is table stakes for an orchestrator: a DAG that can only be launched by a
human at a terminal is a batch script, not a control plane.

BLUT has the seed but not the system. `src/sensor.rs` (the sensor substrate,
landed) can evaluate a `SensorOutcome`, but there is no daemon that runs sensors
on a schedule, no ingress for external events, no notification sink, and no
notion of an SLA (a run that should finish by T, or data that must be no older
than N). Everything is human-initiated.

**Numbering note:** the premier-heavyweight roadmap slotted this work as "0084",
but ADR 0084 is already taken by an unrelated codec decision. This ADR therefore
takes **0094** and supersedes the roadmap's "0084" label for eventing/triggers —
there is no codec/eventing collision; the roadmap number was simply stale.

## Decision

BLUT will build an event/data-driven trigger system in four parts, each
respecting the charter. **(1) Sensor daemon** — `blut sensord`, a long-running
engine process (charter-safe: it links no server) that extends `src/sensor.rs`
with concrete sensor kinds: `file-drop` (a path/glob appears or changes),
`spool` (a watched directory drains/fills past a threshold), and `cron` (a
schedule fires). On a sensor firing, the daemon dispatches a run of a
registered plan (`registry://plan@…`, ADR 0085) through the normal path — broker
admission (ADR 0046/0047) is never bypassed, so a triggered run queues behind
the same envelope as a human one. **(2) Webhook ingress** — lives *only* in the
`blut-web` sidecar (ADR 0083/0093): `POST /events/:trigger` validates a signed
payload and appends an event record the sensor daemon consumes via the same
artifact-tail mechanism the dashboard uses; the engine never listens on a socket
(ADR 0034). **(3) `blut-notify` crate** — a sidecar that tails `status.jsonl`
and routes rule matches to sinks (Slack / Discord / ntfy / SMTP / `exec`); sink
credentials are `SecretRef`s (ADR 0086). **(4) SLA rules** — a declarative rule
file (`max_runtime`, `deadline`, data `freshness`) that both the daemon and
`blut sla check` (a pure lineage-DB read in the engine — charter-fine) evaluate,
writing violations to `sla.jsonl`; a breach is itself an event that can notify or
re-trigger. Clinical hard-block holds at the new ingress: a webhook or sensor
tagged `restricted` (ADR 0061/0096) may only fire a same-tenant plan on the same
box, and `blut-notify` refuses to emit any Restricted payload content off-box —
an SLA breach on a clinical run notifies with a redacted, PHI-free summary only.

## Rationale

- Extending `src/sensor.rs` rather than inventing a scheduler reuses the
  `SensorOutcome` contract and the artifact-tail transport the console/web
  already trust — one event substrate, not two.
- Putting webhook ingress in the sidecar (not the engine) is the only
  charter-legal option (ADR 0034 bans an engine listener); the sensor daemon
  consuming an appended event file keeps the engine a pure file-reader.
- Routing triggered runs through broker admission (ADR 0046) means a flood of
  file-drops or a webhook storm cannot stampede the box — the envelope throttles
  triggered and human runs identically.
- SLA-as-data (a rule file both the daemon and a CLI read) gives CI, the TUI, and
  the daemon the same answer for "is this run late?" — no logic fork.
- `blut-notify` as a separate crate keeps SMTP/HTTP clients out of the engine and
  lets sinks evolve without touching the control plane.

## Alternatives Considered

- **An in-engine cron/scheduler thread with a built-in HTTP webhook listener.**
  Rejected: the webhook listener is an in-engine HTTP server, banned outright by
  ADR 0034; and an in-engine scheduler that dispatches around the broker would
  let a busy cron schedule (or a webhook storm) bypass admission (ADR 0046) and
  OOM the box — the exact failure the broker exists to prevent.
- **Poll external systems from inside each stage (no sensor layer).** Rejected:
  it scatters "wait for the world" logic across every pipeline, gives no central
  place to rate-limit or audit triggers, and means a clinical stage would open
  its own outbound connections — uncontrollable at the ADR-0061 custody boundary.
  A single sensor daemon + sidecar ingress is the one place to gate all inbound
  events.
- **Reuse an off-the-shelf notifier (Alertmanager / Apprise) as a hard
  dependency.** Rejected: it adds a network daemon to operate and cannot enforce
  the clinical redaction rule (PHI-free summaries only) — `blut-notify` must own
  the redaction pass (ADR 0086) so no Restricted content reaches a sink; a
  generic notifier can be an `exec` *sink target*, not the mechanism.

## Consequences

- Upside: BLUT gains sensors, webhooks, cron, alerting, and SLAs — the operator
  feature set that lets it stand next to Airflow/Prefect in an evaluation.
- Upside: triggered runs, SLA breaches, and webhooks are all just events feeding
  the same daemon → uniform audit + broker gating + notification.
- Downside: `blut sensord` is a new long-lived process to supervise (systemd),
  monitor for its own liveness, and reason about at-least-once vs exactly-once
  trigger semantics (a file-drop seen twice must not double-dispatch — dedupe on
  the event's content hash).
- Downside: webhook ingress adds an authenticated public surface on the sidecar
  (signature verification, replay protection) — real security work (leans on ADR
  0095).
- Constraint: SLA freshness rules depend on the lineage DB carrying accurate
  data-timestamps; a stage that lies about output freshness makes SLA checks
  wrong — freshness is only as honest as the provenance rows.

## Implementation Plan  *(the contract — write once; amend only by a dated Progress Log entry)*

- **Deliverable:** `blut sensord` (file-drop/spool/cron sensors over
  `src/sensor.rs`), `POST /events/:trigger` in `blut-web`, the `blut-notify`
  sidecar crate (Slack/Discord/ntfy/SMTP/exec sinks), and an SLA rule file +
  `blut sla check` writing `sla.jsonl`.
- **Acceptance gate (fail-CLOSED; unmeasured ⇒ FAIL):**
  - `gate_cmd:` `cargo test -p blut --test sensor_trigger && cargo test -p
    blut-notify --test sla_notify` — drops a file the sensor watches and asserts
    exactly one broker-admitted run of the registered plan is dispatched (a
    second identical drop does NOT re-dispatch), then forces a `max_runtime`
    breach and asserts an `sla.jsonl` row + one redacted (PHI-free) notification
    for a `restricted` run.
  - `pass when:` `exit == 0` — one dispatch per unique event (dedupe holds),
    every triggered run passed through broker admission, and the clinical
    notification contains no Restricted payload content.
- **Rollback:** the sensor daemon and sidecars are opt-in processes; stopping
  `blut sensord`, `blut-notify`, and the webhook route reverts BLUT to
  human-initiated runs with zero engine change.

## Progress Log  *(append-only; newest last; never rewrite an earlier entry)*

- _2026-07-10 — opened._ Records the numbering correction: eventing/triggers
  takes ADR **0094**, not the roadmap's stale "0084" (already a codec ADR).
- _2026-07-19 — BUILT + FROZEN in three increments (engine `88f1e12` →
  `0ae8994` → `c30d584`; cookbook `8e527dd`)._
  1. **Trigger substrate (incr 1, `88f1e12`)** — `src/trigger.rs`: the
     `Trigger` trait + `FileDropTrigger` (file-drop/spool sensor, content-hash
     event id folding path+size+mtime), a persistent `SeenStore` (at-least-once
     → exactly-once dedupe, survives a daemon restart), and the load-bearing
     `AdmissionDispatcher` — a fired event launches a plan ONLY after
     `broker::admission::decide` admits (ADR 0046/0047 never bypassed); a
     refused event stays eligible (backpressure, not a silent drop). The
     `dispatch → mark-seen-only-on-Admit` rule is the dedupe correctness pin.
  2. **SLA + notify (incr 2, `0ae8994`)** — the keystone `blut_types::sla`
     (`SlaBreach`/`SlaKind`, shared producer↔consumer, wasm32-clean);
     `src/sla.rs` (`SlaRule` max_runtime/deadline/freshness, pure `evaluate`,
     `append_breaches` → `sla.jsonl`, PHI-free summaries by construction);
     `blut-notify` grew `breach_to_envelope`/`read_breaches`/`notify_breaches`
     (custody chokepoint — a restricted breach to an off-box sink is a
     fail-closed drop) and a real `ExecSink` (payload on stdin, never argv).
  3. **Runnable wiring (incr 3, `c30d584`)** — `blut sensord`
     (`--triggers`/`--once`/`--interval`/`--cli`; loads `triggers.toml`, drives
     each binding through the real admission-gated dispatcher, launches
     `<cli> recipe run <plan>` detached); `blut sla check` (a pure lineage read
     over the new `LineageDb::all_runs`, exits 1 iff a breach was written — a
     cron/CI alert gate); and the webhook ingress `POST /api/events/{trigger}`
     in `blut-web` (validates + content-addresses the body into the trigger
     spool the daemon watches — HTTP→filesystem keeps the engine a pure reader,
     ADR 0034). The cookbook pin bump (`8e527dd`) surfaces these as `lqt`
     subcommands.
  Charter held throughout: no engine HTTP listener (ingress is the sidecar);
  triggered runs pass broker admission; the clinical hard-block holds at the
  new ingress (a restricted breach never notifies off-box). Live smoke on the
  box: `lqt sla check` clean; `lqt sensord --once` correctly REFUSED a dropped
  event under real memory pressure (7G free < 2G+6G) — the envelope enforced on
  live state — with the event staying eligible to retry.
- _2026-07-20 — COMPLETION EVIDENCE CORRECTED (engine `df6d312`)._ The
  2026-07-19 freeze entry and completion block recorded the initial substrate
  as the whole frozen contract too early. The named commits did not yet provide
  spool-threshold or cron triggers, signed/replay-bounded webhook
  authentication, an exact child-admission acknowledgement, shared daemon/CLI
  freshness evaluation, declarative notification rules, or runnable
  Slack/Discord/ntfy/SMTP tailing. Commit `df6d312` closes those tails without
  changing the decision: shared validated `triggers.toml`; file/spool/cron
  sources; content-stable dedupe plus durable `.admitted` recovery; launch only
  after the real recipe holds its exact tenant reservation and scheduler lock;
  HMAC-SHA256 webhook ingress with timestamp window, `SecretRef`, custody, and
  content-addressed replay handling; measured fail-closed SLA freshness used by
  both `sensord` and `blut sla check`; and a locked, atomic-cursor notifier with
  Slack/Discord/ntfy/SMTP/exec sinks, redaction, rotation recovery, and
  at-least-once retry. The original gates now pass against the completed
  implementation (`sensor_trigger`, `sla_notify`, and
  `dashboard_readonly`), as do the full locked workspace, standalone web,
  notifier, clippy, rustdoc, wasm, and custody/scope gates. This dated entry is
  the authoritative completion evidence where the earlier result conflicts.

## Completion / Resolution  *(fill once; this + the frozen Status line is the single freeze mark)*

- **verdict:** passed
- **gate_cmd:** `cargo test -p blut --test sensor_trigger && cargo test -p
  blut-notify --test sla_notify` (plus `cargo test -p blut-web --test
  dashboard_readonly` for the webhook ingress; full engine/notify/web suites +
  clippy)
- **result:** `sensor_trigger` green — one broker-admitted dispatch per unique

## Related Decisions

ADR 0083 (sidecars host webhook ingress + `blut-notify`; engine stays
HTTP-free), ADR 0101 (`src/sensor.rs` substrate — this extends it, does not
supersede), ADR 0085 (triggers dispatch registered plans), ADR 0046/0047 (broker

# ADR 0095: Gate every mutating BLUT control action behind capability-scoped tokens (viewer/operator/admin) with an audit trail, defaulting to read-only and opening a path to OIDC

<!-- The title IS this ADR's one-line summary in the generated index/digest. -->

> **This file is append-only and living.** Write the decision once. As
> implementation proceeds, **append** dated entries to the Progress Log — never
> rewrite or delete earlier text; correct an earlier statement with a *new* dated
> entry beneath it, so the original stays as historical record. When the
> deliverable passes its gate, fill **Completion** and set Status to
> `Complete — frozen YYYY-MM-DD`. A frozen ADR is permanent. To reverse a frozen
> decision later, write a *new* ADR that supersedes it (updating this one's
> Status pointer is the only edit allowed after freeze).

## Status

`Proposed 2026-07-10` → `In progress` → `Complete — frozen 2026-07-11`

## Context

Prefect and Dagster+ ship workspace RBAC; Flyte leans on project-scoped IAM.
Once an orchestrator has a web control plane (ADR 0093), "who is allowed to
promote to prod / cancel a run / read a clinical tenant's lineage" stops being a
single-operator assumption and becomes a security boundary an evaluator will
probe.

BLUT has no authz at all. The TUI assumes the one person at the terminal owns the
box; the moment `blut-web` (ADR 0093 v2) and webhook ingress (ADR 0094) expose
mutating actions over the network, an unauthenticated `POST` could launch a run,
rollback a deployment (ADR 0085), or read a Restricted tenant's status. There is
no token, no role, no audit of who did what. This must be closed *before* the web
control plane's write path (v2) ships, and the read path (v1) must default to a
posture that leaks nothing.

## Decision

BLUT will add **capability-scoped auth** enforced at every mutating control
boundary. Three built-in roles, ordered by capability: `viewer` (read status /
lineage / DAG — no mutation), `operator` (viewer + run / cancel / retry), `admin`
(operator + `plan promote`/`rollback`, secret management, tenant + token
administration). Tokens live in `~/.blut/web-tokens.toml` (bcrypt/argon2-hashed
token secrets, never plaintext), each row binding a token to a role and a tenant
(ADR 0096). **Read-only is the default**: an unauthenticated or unrecognised
caller gets `viewer` scope *only* for non-restricted tenants, and any request
without a valid token that targets a mutation or a `restricted` tenant is
refused. **Every mutating action is gated AND audit-logged**: the exec-bridge
(ADR 0083) checks the caller's capability before shelling to the CLI and writes a
`~/.blut/audit.jsonl` row (actor token id, role, tenant, action, target
fingerprint, timestamp, allow/deny) *before* dispatch — a denied action is
logged too. Enforcement is fail-closed: a token that does not resolve to a role,
or a role that does not dominate the action's required capability, is a deny, not
a fallthrough. Clinical hard-block composes on top (ADR 0061/0096): no role,
including `admin`, grants a *shared*-tenant token access to a `restricted`
tenant's data or actions — clinical access requires a token minted in that
tenant, on that box. The token file is the v1 mechanism; the design keeps the
capability check behind a `Principal` trait so an **OIDC** resolver (map an OIDC
group claim → role) can be added later as a sidecar-mediated token exchange
without changing any gate.

## Rationale

- Capability domination (`admin ⊇ operator ⊇ viewer`) is a total order that makes
  each gate a single comparison — simple to audit and impossible to
  half-configure into an accidental grant.
- Read-only default + fail-closed means the *insecure* state is "can't do
  anything," never "can do everything" — the safe failure direction for a control
  plane exposed to the network.
- Gating at the exec-bridge (ADR 0083) reuses the single enforcement path humans
  and the web share, so authz cannot be bypassed by a second mutation route (ADR
  0093 forbids one existing anyway).
- Audit-before-dispatch (including denies) gives the tamper-evident "who did
  what" trail RBAC exists to provide, and it is the same `audit.jsonl` the plan
  registry (ADR 0085) and secrets (ADR 0086) actions write to — one trail.
- A `Principal` trait behind the token file means OIDC is an additive resolver,
  not a rewrite — we ship the simple thing now without painting out the
  enterprise path.

## Alternatives Considered

- **OS-user / unix-socket peer-credential auth only (trust whoever can reach the
  box).** Rejected: it collapses the moment `blut-web` serves over a network
  socket to browsers that have no OS identity on the host, and it cannot express
  "this operator may run but not promote to prod" or the clinical tenant boundary
  — peer-cred is coarse machine-level trust, not per-action capability.
- **Full OIDC/SSO from day one.** Rejected: it requires standing up (or
  depending on) an external identity provider before *any* authz exists, blocking
  the ADR-0093 v2 write path on enterprise infrastructure most single-team
  deployments don't have; the token file gives real authz immediately and OIDC
  slots in behind the same `Principal` trait later.
- **Per-endpoint ACL lists instead of ordered roles.** Rejected: free-form ACLs
  make "is this caller allowed?" an unbounded set-membership question that is easy
  to misconfigure into an over-grant and hard to audit; three dominating roles
  keep every decision a single comparison and every token's power obvious from its
  role name.

## Consequences

- Upside: the web control plane (ADR 0093 v2) and webhook ingress (ADR 0094) can
  ship a write path safely; mutations are gated and attributable.
- Upside: one `audit.jsonl` becomes the compliance substrate for registry,
  secrets, and control actions — a single tamper-evident log to review.
- Downside: token issuance/rotation is a new operator responsibility; a lost
  `admin` token or a botched `web-tokens.toml` can lock out mutation (recoverable
  only by local file edit on the box — an intentional last-resort).
- Downside: every mutating code path now takes a `Principal` and a capability
  check — a cross-cutting change touching the exec-bridge and every control
  subcommand; a missing check is a silent authz hole, so the gate test must
  enumerate mutating actions.
- Constraint: `viewer`-default read access still must honour tenant scoping —
  the default viewer sees only non-restricted tenants, never all data.

## Implementation Plan  *(the contract — write once; amend only by a dated Progress Log entry)*

- **Deliverable:** a `Principal` + capability model, `~/.blut/web-tokens.toml`
  (hashed tokens → role + tenant), gate checks on every mutating control action,
  and `~/.blut/audit.jsonl` allow/deny records; an OIDC-resolver seam behind the
  `Principal` trait.
- **Acceptance gate (fail-CLOSED; unmeasured ⇒ FAIL):**
  - `gate_cmd:` `cargo test -p blut --test rbac_matrix` — drives each mutating
    action (`run`, `cancel`, `plan promote`, `plan rollback`, `secret set`) with a
    `viewer`, `operator`, and `admin` token and with no token, asserting the
    allow/deny matrix, that a `restricted`-tenant action is denied to every
    shared-tenant token including `admin`, and that every attempt (allow and deny)
    produced an `audit.jsonl` row.
  - `pass when:` `exit == 0` — matrix matches the role order exactly, clinical
    cross-tenant is always denied, and the audit row count equals the attempt
    count.
- **Rollback:** auth is behind a `--features rbac` gate defaulting on for
  `blut-web`; disabling it reverts to single-operator TUI trust (no network
  write path), so the fallback is "no web mutation," never "open web mutation."

## Progress Log  *(append-only; newest last; never rewrite an earlier entry)*

- _2026-07-10 — opened._
- _2026-07-11 — LANDED + FROZEN (engine main `f9de1d0`). `src/rbac.rs`: `Role`
  {Viewer<Operator<Admin} (derived `Ord` = the single capability order); `Action`
  → `required_role` (read=viewer, run/cancel/retry=operator, plan
  promote/rollback + secret/token/tenant admin=admin); `Principal{token_id, role,
  tenant}`; fail-closed `authorize` (read-only default — anonymous = viewer on

# ADR 0096: Give BLUT projects/domains with per-tenant namespaces for cache, registry, and plans — and make the clinical zone a hard tenant boundary a Restricted tenant's data can never cross

<!-- The title IS this ADR's one-line summary in the generated index/digest. -->

> **This file is append-only and living.** Write the decision once. As
> implementation proceeds, **append** dated entries to the Progress Log — never
> rewrite or delete earlier text; correct an earlier statement with a *new* dated
> entry beneath it, so the original stays as historical record. When the
> deliverable passes its gate, fill **Completion** and set Status to
> `Complete — frozen YYYY-MM-DD`. A frozen ADR is permanent. To reverse a frozen
> decision later, write a *new* ADR that supersedes it (updating this one's
> Status pointer is the only edit allowed after freeze).

## Status

`Proposed 2026-07-10` → `In progress` → `Complete — frozen 2026-07-13`
(engine `550f910`)

## Context

Flyte's projects + domains are the axis every other capability hangs off:
resource quotas, access control, and workflow isolation are all scoped to a
`(project, domain)`. It is what lets one Flyte cluster serve many teams and a
dev/staging/prod split without cross-contamination. No premier orchestrator
ships without a tenancy model.

BLUT has none — this is genuine white-space (nowhere in the roadmap is it
planned). Today the content-addressed cache (ADR 0078), the plan registry (ADR
0085), lineage, and the ε-ledger (ADR 0080) are one flat global namespace on the
box; every run shares one cache, one set of plan pointers, one quota (the broker
envelope, ADR 0046). For a research box that is fine. For a system that also
processes clinical/PHI data under a hard-block (ADR 0061), a *flat* namespace is
actively dangerous: a clinical run's cached intermediate artifact sits in the same
content-addressed store a shared run reads, and a shared `prod` pointer could
point at a clinical fingerprint. The clinical block is currently enforced per
dispatch, but there is no *structural* boundary keeping Restricted artifacts out
of shared namespaces.

## Decision

BLUT will introduce **tenants** (a Flyte-style `project`, optionally with a
`domain` suffix, e.g. `research/dev`, `clinical/prod`) as the top-level isolation
axis, and namespace the three stateful stores by tenant: the content-addressed
cache (`~/.blut/cache/<tenant>/…`, keyed by `(tenant, plan_fingerprint)` — the
ADR-0078 key algorithm is **unchanged**, tenant is a namespace *prefix* on the
store path, not a change to the fingerprint), the plan registry (ADR 0085
pointers are `(tenant, name)` — there is no global `prod`, only
`clinical/prod`, `research/prod`, …), and plans/lineage/ε-ledger rows carry a
`tenant` column. Each tenant gets a **quota** — a broker sub-envelope (ADR
0046/0047) capping its concurrent resource claim, so one tenant cannot starve
another; admission is never bypassed, it is now per-tenant. **The clinical zone
is a HARD boundary, not a soft label**: a tenant marked `restricted` (ADR 0061)
is a sealed namespace — its cache is never read by a non-restricted tenant, its
plan fingerprints can never be promoted onto a shared pointer (ADR 0085), its
lineage/ε rows are never served to a shared-tenant session (ADR 0093/0095), and
mesh replication (ADR 0079) and every sidecar refuse to move a Restricted
artifact off the owning box. The boundary is enforced fail-closed at **every**
dispatch/gate/registry/cache/mesh boundary: a cross-tenant read of a `restricted`
namespace, or any operation that would place a Restricted artifact in a shared
namespace, is a hard deny, logged (ADR 0095), with no fallthrough. Cross-tenant
cache sharing between *non*-restricted tenants is disallowed by default (a run in
tenant A cannot reuse tenant B's cached node) to prevent accidental provenance
bleed; an explicit, audited `shared/` tenant is the only place deliberately
common artifacts live.

## Rationale

- Namespacing the store *path* by tenant while leaving the ADR-0078 fingerprint
  algorithm untouched keeps cache correctness (the key still identifies the graph)
  while giving structural isolation — one prefix, zero change to the hash we've
  already validated.
- Making the clinical zone a *namespace* (not just a per-dispatch check) turns the
  ADR-0061 block from "enforced everywhere we remembered" into "a Restricted
  artifact structurally cannot exist in a shared store" — the boundary is a
  property of where bytes live, which is far harder to leak past than a scattered
  runtime check.
- Per-tenant broker sub-envelopes give real quota (Flyte parity) by reusing the
  admission mechanism already trusted to prevent OOM (ADR 0046) — no new resource
  governor.
- Tenant is the column RBAC (ADR 0095) already binds tokens to, so authz and
  isolation share one axis instead of two overlapping ones.
- Default-no-cross-tenant-sharing fails safe: the accident direction is "we
  recomputed a node we could have reused," never "tenant A read tenant B's data."

## Alternatives Considered

- **Separate BLUT installs / separate boxes per tenant (physical isolation
  only).** Rejected: it gives isolation but throws away the shared broker,
  shared mesh, and single control plane that make BLUT one system — and it still
  doesn't answer the in-box clinical/shared split on a research box that
  occasionally touches PHI. Physical separation is a *deployment* an operator can
  still choose; it is not a substitute for an in-engine tenancy model.
- **A soft `tenant` label on rows with no namespaced stores (filter, don't
  isolate).** Rejected: a filter-based boundary means a Restricted artifact
  physically sits in the shared content-addressed cache and is one missing
  `WHERE tenant=` clause away from being served — exactly the leak ADR 0061
  forbids. The clinical boundary must be structural (separate store paths, refused
  at replication), not a query predicate.
- **Reuse Linux namespaces / cgroups as the tenant boundary.** Rejected: those
  isolate *processes and resources* but not the *logical* stores (cache, registry,
  lineage) that must be tenant-scoped, and the broker already owns cgroup
  containment (ADR 0046); tenancy is a data-namespacing concern layered above
  containment, not the same thing.

## Consequences

- Upside: BLUT can serve multiple teams and a dev/prod split on one box with real
  quota, and the clinical block becomes a structural namespace boundary instead of
  a runtime check repeated at each site — much stronger custody.
- Upside: RBAC (ADR 0095), the registry (ADR 0085), and the ε-ledger (ADR 0080)
  all gain their scoping axis "for free" — they already needed `tenant`.
- Downside: every store path, every registry pointer, and many DB queries grow a
  tenant dimension — a wide, migration-heavy change; a query that forgets the
  tenant scope is an isolation bug, so the gate must probe cross-tenant reads
  directly.
- Downside: default-no-cross-tenant cache sharing costs recompute when two
  non-restricted tenants genuinely run the same graph; the explicit `shared/`
  tenant is the escape hatch, at the price of an audited opt-in.
- Constraint locked: no future feature (mesh, web, notify, sensors) may move a
  `restricted` artifact off its owning box or into a shared namespace — this ADR
  is the structural statement of ADR 0061 that all of them must honour.

## Implementation Plan  *(the contract — write once; amend only by a dated Progress Log entry)*

- **Deliverable:** a `Tenant` (`project[/domain]`) axis; tenant-prefixed cache /
  registry / plan / lineage / ε namespaces; per-tenant broker sub-envelopes; and
  a fail-closed clinical-zone boundary refused at dispatch, cache, registry,
  mesh, and sidecar surfaces.
- **Acceptance gate (fail-CLOSED; unmeasured ⇒ FAIL):**
  - `gate_cmd:` `cargo test -p blut --test tenant_isolation` — runs the same
    graph in tenant `research/dev` and `clinical/prod`, asserts their cache
    entries live in disjoint store paths and neither reads the other's; asserts
    promoting the `clinical/prod` fingerprint onto a `research/prod` pointer is
    denied; asserts the mesh-replication and `blut-notify` paths refuse the
    `restricted` artifact; and asserts the ADR-0078 fingerprint of the graph is
    byte-identical across the two tenants (namespacing changed the path, not the
    key).
  - `pass when:` `exit == 0` — disjoint cache paths, cross-tenant read denied,
    clinical→shared promote/replicate/notify all return non-zero, fingerprint
    unchanged across tenants.
- **Rollback:** default tenant is a single `default/` namespace; with one tenant
  configured the system behaves exactly as the current flat store (the prefix is a
  constant), so tenancy can be disabled by pinning every run to `default/`.

## Progress Log  *(append-only; newest last; never rewrite an earlier entry)*

- _2026-07-10 — opened._
