# ADR 0106: Make the scheduler capability highly available via Raft — leader election and replicated scheduler state that survives a coordinator crash without losing in-flight dispatch

> **This file is append-only and living.** Write the decision once. As
> implementation proceeds, **append** dated entries to the Progress Log — never
> rewrite earlier text. When the deliverable passes its gate, fill
> **Completion** and set Status to `Complete — frozen YYYY-MM-DD`.

## Status

Proposed 2026-07-10. Group 5 (distributed scale). **Extends ADR 0079 (symmetric
mesh) and ADR 0082 (cloud queue); does not supersede either.** ADR 0079 already
made "scheduler" a *capability* any node may enable and explicitly deferred HA to
"a separate, later concern (ADR 0067 T3.4)" — this is that concern. The mesh
transport, trust matrix, and clinical hard-block are unchanged; this ADR only
replicates the scheduler capability's *state* across a quorum of scheduler-capable
nodes.

## Context

ADR 0079 left the scheduler as a single logical decision-maker: even though every
node *can* run one, a given DAG is driven by one node's `Coordinator`/dispatch
matrix at a time. If that node crashes mid-run, the in-flight dispatch table
(which stages are RUNNING on which peers, which are QUEUED, the reputation EMAs)
is lost — surviving workers keep computing but no one collects their results, and
a restart re-dispatches already-running stages, double-billing the cloud queue
(0082) and violating content-addressed idempotency expectations. Temporal and
Airflow solve this with an HA scheduler backed by a replicated store; BLUT has
the mesh but no replicated *scheduler* state and no leader election, so there is
no principled failover. The charter forbids an in-engine HTTP server and any new
always-on network service must ride the existing mesh, so an external etcd/
ZooKeeper is off the table.

## Decision

Replicate the scheduler capability's state with an **embedded Raft group** running
over the mesh transport. Scheduler-capable nodes form a Raft cluster (odd-sized,
operator-declared members — not open gossip membership, so a random gossiped peer
cannot join the quorum); the **leader** owns dispatch, followers hot-stand-by. The
replicated state machine is exactly the scheduler's durable facts: the DAG's
per-stage status (`QUEUED/DISPATCHED/RUNNING/DONE/FAILED`), the stage→peer
assignment, the content-addressed result keys, and cloud-queue job handles (0082).
Every dispatch decision is a Raft log entry committed by quorum *before* the
`Task` frame goes out over the mesh, so a committed "stage X dispatched to peer P
with expected `blake3=…`" survives leader loss. On failover the new leader
**reconciles rather than re-dispatches**: it queries live peers for the status of
each `DISPATCHED/RUNNING` stage over the mesh, adopts any already-complete result
by its content hash (idempotent — the key is unchanged, per charter), and only
re-dispatches stages with no live owner and no committed result. Raft runs as an
**embedded library over mesh bi-streams** (charter: no HTTP, no separate service);
consensus messages are just another authenticated `MeshFrame` type. The clinical
hard-block is untouched — Raft replicates *scheduler metadata* (stage status,
content-hash keys, peer ids), never `Restricted` data or gradients, which never
enter the log.

## Rationale

- **Commit-before-dispatch is the whole trick.** If the dispatch decision is in the
  quorum-committed log before the task leaves, no failover can forget a running
  stage; reconcile-not-re-dispatch then makes recovery idempotent because result
  keys are content-addressed (unchanged, per charter).
- **Reuse the mesh; add no service.** Raft is a library, its RPCs are `MeshFrame`s
  over the already-mTLS bi-stream — no HTTP, no etcd, charter intact.
- **Closed membership for the quorum.** Gossip (0079 A5) is fine for *worker*
  discovery but a consensus quorum must not admit a gossiped stranger — operator-
  declared members keep Sybil nodes out of the vote that controls dispatch.
- **Metadata-only replication** keeps the clinical hard-block trivially true: the
  log holds status and hashes, never PHI or gradients.

## Alternatives Considered

- **External etcd / ZooKeeper for scheduler state.** Rejected — a separate
  always-on clustered service to secure and operate, reachable off-mesh, which the
  charter's "no new network service outside the mesh" spirit and the no-HTTP rule
  push back on. Embedded Raft over the mesh keeps one transport and one trust root.
- **Primary/backup with a shared object-store checkpoint (no consensus).** Rejected
  — periodic checkpointing loses every dispatch decision since the last snapshot,
  reintroducing the double-dispatch window this ADR exists to close; and split-brain
  (two nodes both think they're primary) has no principled resolution without a
  consensus term/leader.
- **Stateless re-run on failover (recompute the whole DAG).** Rejected — for a
  multi-hour codec joint train that re-runs already-complete, cloud-billed stages;
  content-addressed keys make adoption cheap, so throwing that away is pure waste.

## Consequences

- Scheduler-capable nodes gain a Raft state machine and an operator-declared member
  list; single-node deployments run a trivial 1-member Raft (no behavior change,
  no quorum wait).
- Dispatch latency gains one quorum-commit round-trip per decision — bounded and
  worth it for exactly-once dispatch; the software gate measures it.
- The cloud queue (0082) job-handle lifecycle is now replicated, closing the
  double-bill-on-crash hole.
- A new failure mode (loss of quorum → no dispatch) is by design: fail-closed, the
  cluster refuses to dispatch rather than risk split-brain double-dispatch.

## Implementation Plan  *(the contract — write once; amend only by a dated Progress Log entry)*

- **Deliverable:** an embedded Raft group over the mesh replicating scheduler state,
  with commit-before-dispatch and reconcile-not-re-dispatch failover.
- **Acceptance gate (fail-CLOSED; unmeasured ⇒ FAIL):**
  - **Software (CI, non-HW — in-process multi-node harness):**
    - `gate_cmd:` `cargo test -p blut --features "p2p raft" ha_failover_no_double_dispatch`
    - `pass when:` `exit==0` — with 3 in-process scheduler nodes, killing the leader
      mid-DAG causes a follower to win election, adopt already-complete stages by
      content hash, re-dispatch **only** orphaned stages (assert each stage
      dispatched at most once across the whole run), and lose no committed result;
      and loss of quorum halts dispatch (fail-closed) rather than proceeding.
  - **HARDWARE-GATED (≥3 real nodes; multi-node bringup required):**
    - `gate_cmd:` `bash tools/scripts/ha_chaos.sh --nodes 3 --kill-leader --dag codec_joint`
    - `pass when:` on real hardware, a leader kill during a live DAG produces exactly
      one successful completion per stage with zero cloud double-bills (0082 ledger
      cross-check). Recorded in the tier-4 hardware validation ledger.
- **Rollback:** disable the `raft` feature; scheduler reverts to 0079's single
  driver (no HA, crash loses in-flight table as before). No data or checkpoint at
  risk; content-addressed keys make a manual re-run safe.

## Progress Log  *(append-only; newest last; never rewrite an earlier entry)*

- _2026-07-10 — opened._
- _2026-07-12 — M2.0 CONTROL REPAIR: planning contract only. The engine has no
  `raft` feature or named `ha_failover_no_double_dispatch` target, and
  `tools/scripts/ha_chaos.sh` is absent. No quorum/failover measurement has run;
  the current scheduler remains single-driver as this ADR's rollback describes._

## Completion / Resolution  *(fill once; this + the frozen Status line is the single freeze mark)*

- **gate_cmd:** —
- **result:** —

## Related Decisions

ADR 0079 (symmetric mesh — scheduler capability + deferred HA), ADR 0082 (cloud
queue — replicated job handles), ADR 0034 (no-HTTP charter — Raft rides the mesh).

## Validation  *(ongoing — distinct from the completion gate above)*

Watch the dispatch double-fire counter and the cloud-queue double-bill ledger on
every real failover — either going non-zero means commit-before-dispatch or
reconcile has a hole and forces a fix. Watch quorum-commit latency as the member
count grows; if it dominates dispatch time the member set is too large for the
deployment and should be re-scoped.

# ADR 0107: Add geo-aware dispatch, a bandwidth-aware global cache tier, and hard compliance zones — the clinical zone is a geo boundary PHI never crosses

> **This file is append-only and living.** Write the decision once. As
> implementation proceeds, **append** dated entries to the Progress Log — never
> rewrite earlier text. When the deliverable passes its gate, fill
> **Completion** and set Status to `Complete — frozen YYYY-MM-DD`.

## Status

Proposed 2026-07-10. Group 5 (distributed scale) — the 100-datacenter tier.
**Extends ADR 0061 (P2P trust/clinical hard-block), ADR 0106 (HA control plane),
and ADR 0096; does not supersede any.** ADR 0061's clinical hard-block is
*hardened into a geo boundary* here, not relaxed; the trust matrix, content-
addressed cache keys, and mesh transport are unchanged.

## Context

ADRs 0104–0106 scale training across GPUs, nodes, and an HA control plane, but all
of that assumes a single locality. The roadmap's 100-datacenter vision
(project_blut_scaling_validation) puts nodes in many regions with wildly different
inter-region bandwidth/RTT and, critically, **different data-residency
jurisdictions**. Two problems appear at geo scale that node-local logic does not
solve: (1) dispatch and cache transfer that ignore geography will route a stage's
inputs across an expensive, slow trans-region link when a same-region replica
exists — and re-fetch the 46 GB window cache per region; (2) **compliance** —
clinical/PHI data (0061) governed by data-residency law must be provably confined
to an authorized region. Today the clinical hard-block is enforced per *trust
level* (weights/gradients never leave a node for `Restricted` data); at geo scale
that must be lifted to a *zone* invariant: `Restricted` data, its derived
artifacts, and its cache chunks must never be dispatched to, replicated to, or
cached in a node outside its declared compliance zone — a hard geographic
boundary, fail-closed.

## Decision

Add a **compliance-zone** attribute to every node (operator-declared, signed into
the registry like 0079 A4 identity — a node cannot self-assert a zone it was not
provisioned into) and a **`GeoTopology`** view (region, inter-zone bandwidth/RTT,
reusing ADR 0105's `NetTopology` probe). Three coupled mechanisms, all fail-closed:

1. **Geo-aware dispatch.** The scheduler (0106 leader) ranks candidate peers for a
   stage by region locality and measured bandwidth, preferring same-zone / same-
   region peers and treating a cross-region hop as a cost, not a default.
2. **Bandwidth-aware global cache tier.** The content-addressed object store gains
   a **per-zone replica index**: a chunk is fetched from the nearest zone that
   already holds it (by content hash — keys unchanged, per charter), and a
   region's cache is populated once then shared locally, killing the per-region
   46 GB re-fetch. Replica placement is bandwidth-aware (seed to a region only when
   a stage there needs it).
3. **Compliance zones as hard geo boundaries.** Each `DataClass` carries an
   **allowed-zone set**; `Restricted`/PHI's set is its single provisioned clinical
   zone. The dispatcher **refuses** to place a `Restricted` stage on any node
   outside that zone; the cache tier **refuses** to replicate or cache a
   `Restricted` chunk into any out-of-zone node; and gradients/derived artifacts
   inherit the source data's zone. A stage whose zone cannot be satisfied is
   refused, never silently downgraded to a permissive zone. This is enforced at
   *both* the dispatch decision (0106 Raft, so the refusal is replicated and
   auditable) and the transfer layer (a receiving node rejects an out-of-zone
   `Restricted` chunk fail-closed), so a single-layer bug cannot leak PHI across a
   boundary.

The clinical zone is therefore a **geo wall**: `Restricted` data, its cache chunks,
its gradients, and any artifact derived from it are physically confined to the
authorized region. Non-restricted classes (public corpora, synthetic) may use the
global cache tier and cross-region dispatch freely.

## Rationale

- **Zone must be signed, not self-asserted.** A node claiming "I am in the clinical
  zone" without a provisioned, signed attestation is exactly the leak vector;
  binding zone to the 0079 signed registry closes it.
- **Two-layer enforcement (dispatch + transfer).** Defense in depth: even if a
  dispatch bug picks an out-of-zone node, the receiver rejects the restricted chunk.
  PHI containment is too important for a single check.
- **Content-hash replicas make the global cache safe *and* cheap.** Keys are
  unchanged (charter), so a chunk in region A and region B are provably identical;
  per-zone replicas kill the re-fetch without weakening idempotency.
- **Refuse, never downgrade.** A stage that cannot run in a compliant zone must
  halt visibly — silently running it elsewhere is the failure mode data-residency
  law exists to prevent.
- **Enforced through the Raft leader (0106)** so every zone refusal is a replicated,
  auditable fact, not a transient local decision.

## Alternatives Considered

- **Encrypt-and-replicate PHI everywhere, rely on crypto for compliance.** Rejected
  — data-residency law is about *physical location*, not just confidentiality;
  encrypted PHI bytes sitting on an out-of-region disk still violate residency, and
  0061's hard-block is a location invariant, not an encryption one. Zones must be a
  geographic boundary.
- **Soft geo-affinity (prefer local, allow spillover under load).** Rejected for the
  restricted class — "allow spillover" is precisely a PHI-crosses-border event; soft
  affinity is fine for public data but the clinical zone must be hard. We keep soft
  affinity only for non-restricted classes.
- **A central compliance service that vets every dispatch.** Rejected — a new
  always-on service (charter: no in-engine HTTP; ride the mesh/Raft), and a single
  chokepoint; enforcing at the replicated scheduler + the transfer layer distributes
  it without a new service.

## Consequences

- Every node gains a signed compliance-zone attribute; deployments that don't set
  it default to a single implicit zone (no behavior change for single-region users).
- The object store gains a per-zone replica index; cache keys are unchanged, so
  existing archives are compatible.
- The restricted class is now confined to one region — a documented, fail-closed
  legal requirement, and it means cross-region acceleration is unavailable to
  clinical training (consistent with 0105's single-node restriction).
- Geo/zone logic is loopback-simulatable (nodes tagged with synthetic zones); the
  real 100-DC behavior is hardware/multi-region gated.

## Implementation Plan  *(the contract — write once; amend only by a dated Progress Log entry)*

- **Deliverable:** signed compliance zones + geo-aware dispatch + per-zone content-
  addressed cache replicas, with two-layer fail-closed refusal of any out-of-zone
  `Restricted` placement, cache, or transfer.
- **Acceptance gate (fail-CLOSED; unmeasured ⇒ FAIL):**
  - **Software (CI, non-HW — simulated multi-zone mesh):**
    - `gate_cmd:` `cargo test -p blut --features "p2p raft geo" restricted_never_crosses_zone`
    - `pass when:` `exit==0` — a `Restricted` stage is refused every out-of-zone
      node at the dispatch layer AND the transfer layer independently rejects an
      out-of-zone restricted chunk; a node with an unsigned/forged zone is dropped
      fail-closed; and a non-restricted chunk is fetched from the nearest zone
      holding it (replica-index hit assertion, zero cross-zone re-fetch when a local
      replica exists).
  - **HARDWARE-GATED (≥2 regions / multi-DC bringup required):**
    - `gate_cmd:` `bash tools/scripts/geo_compliance_audit.sh --zones clinical,public --nodes 4`
    - `pass when:` a real multi-region deployment shows, via an independent audit of
      per-node disk + dispatch logs, zero `Restricted` bytes and zero restricted-
      derived artifacts on any out-of-zone node, and the global cache serves cross-
      region public chunks with no full re-fetch. Recorded in the tier-4 hardware
      validation ledger.
- **Rollback:** disable the `geo` feature — all nodes collapse to one implicit zone,
  cross-region cache replicas off, dispatch geo-agnostic. The 0061/0105 per-node
  clinical hard-block still holds, so PHI is never *less* protected than before this
  ADR; only the geo-cache acceleration is lost.

## Progress Log  *(append-only; newest last; never rewrite an earlier entry)*

- _2026-07-10 — opened._
- _2026-07-12 — M2.0 CONTROL REPAIR: planning contract only. The engine has no
  `raft` or `geo` feature, no named `restricted_never_crosses_zone` target, and
  `tools/scripts/geo_compliance_audit.sh` is absent. Restricted data therefore
  stays node-local under current policy; signed same-zone movement is deferred
  until the M6 audit. No geo-compliance gate has run._

## Completion / Resolution  *(fill once; this + the frozen Status line is the single freeze mark)*

- **verdict:** —
- **gate_cmd:** —
- **result:** —
- **git_sha:** —  ·  **artifact sha256:** —

## Related Decisions

ADR 0061 (clinical hard-block — hardened to a geo boundary), ADR 0106 (Raft leader
enforces + replicates zone refusals), ADR 0096, ADR 0105 (`NetTopology` probe
reused for `GeoTopology`).

## Validation  *(ongoing — distinct from the completion gate above)*

Run the geo-compliance audit continuously, not just at the gate: any `Restricted`
byte found on an out-of-zone disk is a fail-open breach that must halt the mesh and
force an incident ADR. Watch cross-region cache re-fetch volume — if a region keeps
re-fetching chunks a neighbor holds, the replica index or bandwidth ranking is
mis-tuned. Re-audit zone-signing whenever the registry/identity scheme changes.

# ADR 0108: Route the cloud queue across multiple providers with spot/on-demand selection and per-provider billing — extend the single-provider cloud queue

> **This file is append-only and living.** Write the decision once. As
> implementation proceeds, **append** dated entries to the Progress Log — never
> rewrite earlier text. When the deliverable passes its gate, fill
> **Completion** and set Status to `Complete — frozen YYYY-MM-DD`.

## Status

Proposed 2026-07-10. Group 5 (distributed scale). **Extends ADR 0082 (cloud
compute queue) and ADR 0098; does not supersede either.** ADR 0082's submit-job →
get-result-billed-on-compute contract, its P2P data plane + object store, and its
clinical hard-block are unchanged — this ADR only replaces the *single provider*
assumption with a routed set of providers.

## Decision

Add a **provider-routing layer** in front of the ADR 0082 cloud queue. Each cloud
target is a `Provider` descriptor `{name, regions, instance_catalog, spot_supported,
price_fn, account_credential}` (RemoteJob's Slurm+Ray backends are just two more
providers). A job's recipe declares a `cloud_policy` — `{min_gpu, max_price_per_gpu_hr,
allow_spot, deadline, provider_allowlist}` — and the router selects a
(provider, region, instance, spot|on-demand) tuple that satisfies it, ranked by
effective price with spot preferred when `allow_spot` and the job is checkpointable
(durable-resume, Phase D, project_durable_resume). On a spot **preemption** the
router reschedules from the last durable checkpoint onto the next-best tuple —
possibly a different provider — reusing 0082's object-store artifacts by content
hash (keys unchanged, per charter) so no recompute of completed stages. Billing is
**per-provider and per-job**: each provider's spend is attributed to the submitting
job's handle (the 0106-replicated handle), so a multi-provider run produces one
itemized cost ledger, and the daily/weekly `max_price` caps are enforced *before*
dispatch (fail-closed: a job that cannot be placed under its price cap is refused,
never dispatched at any price). Credentials stay **per-provider account only** —
the tail dependency 0082 already noted; the router holds no provider's keys beyond
what that provider's account grants. The **clinical hard-block is absolute**: a
`Restricted`/PHI job is never eligible for *any* external cloud provider (0082 +
0107), so provider routing simply never sees it — restricted training stays on the
owned/clinical-zone fleet, fail-closed.

## Context

ADR 0082 landed a working cloud queue but against a **single provider**: one
account, one region catalog, no spot/on-demand choice, no price-driven selection,
and billing that assumes one bill. At the 100-DC scale (0107) and under real cost
pressure, single-provider is both a availability risk (one provider's capacity/
outage stalls the queue) and a cost bug (paying on-demand when a 3× cheaper spot
instance on another provider would finish a checkpointable job by its deadline).
The pieces to fix it already exist — durable resume makes spot preemption
survivable, the object store makes cross-provider artifact reuse free, and 0106
replicates the job handle billing rides on — so the missing layer is provider
selection and per-provider accounting, not new infrastructure.

## Rationale

- **Spot needs durable resume, which we have.** Preferring spot for checkpointable
  jobs is only safe because Phase-D durable resume + content-addressed artifacts let
  a preempted job restart on another tuple with zero recompute; without that, spot
  would be a footgun, so this ADR is correctly *downstream* of durable resume.
- **Price cap enforced pre-dispatch, fail-closed.** A run that silently blows its
  budget is worse than one that refuses to start; the cap is a placement
  precondition, not a post-hoc alert.
- **Per-provider billing on the replicated handle** gives one itemized ledger across
  providers and closes the double-bill hole (0106) at multi-provider scale.
- **Credentials stay per-account.** The router federates *selection*, not secrets —
  it never becomes a credential aggregator, keeping the blast radius of any one
  provider account bounded (the tail dependency 0082 flagged).
- **Restricted never reaches the router.** The clinical hard-block short-circuits
  before provider selection, so no code path can place PHI on an external provider.

## Alternatives Considered

- **SkyPilot as the cross-cloud broker.** Rejected as the engine's router —
  adopting it pulls an external control layer and its own YAML/launcher stack into
  BLUT's dispatch path, duplicating the 0082 queue and 0106 handle lifecycle, and it
  is opinionated about provisioning in ways the charter's own object-store/mesh data
  plane does not need. We keep routing native and thin (a selection function over
  provider descriptors) and can *target* SkyPilot-managed clusters as one provider
  if ever useful.
- **On-demand only (no spot).** Rejected — leaves the single largest cost lever
  (spot is routinely 3–5× cheaper) on the table for exactly the long checkpointable
  training jobs that dominate spend; durable resume makes spot safe, so refusing it
  is unjustified. Kept as the default for non-checkpointable jobs only.
- **A single aggregated cloud credential/broker account.** Rejected — one credential
  spanning providers is a larger breach blast radius and contradicts 0082's per-
  account tail; per-provider credentials keep each account's exposure bounded.

## Consequences

- The cloud queue gains a provider-routing layer and per-provider `Provider`
  descriptors; single-provider deployments run with a one-element provider set (no
  behavior change).
- Recipes gain a `cloud_policy` block; jobs without one default to 0082's single
  provider, on-demand.
- The billing ledger becomes multi-provider and itemized per job handle (0106).
- Spot preemption handling becomes load-bearing on durable resume — a job declared
  spot-eligible but *not* actually checkpointable is a config error the router must
  reject (asserted in the gate).
- The restricted class never touches external providers — documented, fail-closed,
  consistent with 0105/0107.

## Implementation Plan  *(the contract — write once; amend only by a dated Progress Log entry)*

- **Deliverable:** a provider-routing layer over the ADR 0082 queue — price/deadline
  selection across providers, spot-with-preemption-reschedule for checkpointable
  jobs, per-provider per-job billing on the replicated handle, and a hard clinical
  short-circuit.
- **Acceptance gate (fail-CLOSED; unmeasured ⇒ FAIL):**
  - **Software (CI, non-HW — mock provider catalog + fault injector):**
    - `gate_cmd:` `cargo test -p blut --features cloud multiprovider_route_spot_and_billing`
    - `pass when:` `exit==0` — the router picks the cheapest tuple satisfying a
      `cloud_policy`; a job over its `max_price` cap is refused pre-dispatch (not
      dispatched at any price); an injected spot preemption reschedules from the last
      durable checkpoint onto the next tuple with zero recompute (artifact-hash
      reuse asserted); a spot-eligible-but-not-checkpointable job is rejected as a
      config error; a `Restricted` job never reaches provider selection; and the
      per-provider billing ledger sums to the expected itemized total with no
      double-bill.
  - **HARDWARE-GATED (≥2 real provider accounts; live spot bringup required):**
    - `gate_cmd:` `bash tools/scripts/multiprovider_live.sh --providers a,b --allow-spot --deadline 2h`
    - `pass when:` a real job routed across two live provider accounts completes under
      its price cap and deadline, survives a real spot preemption via durable-resume
      reschedule, and produces one itemized per-provider bill matching each
      provider's own console. Recorded in the tier-4 hardware validation ledger.
- **Rollback:** disable the routing layer — the queue reverts to ADR 0082's single
  provider, on-demand, one bill. No job state at risk; content-addressed artifacts
  and the 0106 handle are provider-agnostic.

## Progress Log  *(append-only; newest last; never rewrite an earlier entry)*

- _2026-07-10 — opened._
- _2026-07-12 — M2.0 CONTROL REPAIR: the base `cloud` feature exists, but the
  named `multiprovider_route_spot_and_billing` target and
  `tools/scripts/multiprovider_live.sh` do not. Multi-provider routing and live
  billing remain proposed; the current cloud queue must not be described as
  proving them._

## Completion / Resolution  *(fill once; this + the frozen Status line is the single freeze mark)*

- **verdict:** —
- **gate_cmd:** —
- **result:** —
- **git_sha:** —  ·  **artifact sha256:** —

## Related Decisions

ADR 0082 (single-provider cloud queue — extended here), ADR 0098, ADR 0106
(replicated job handle carries billing), ADR 0107 (clinical zone bars external
providers for `Restricted`), project_durable_resume (spot-preemption survival).

## Validation  *(ongoing — distinct from the completion gate above)*

Reconcile the router's per-provider ledger against each provider's own console
periodically — a drift means a billing-attribution bug. Watch spot preemption
recompute cost: if a preempted job ever recomputes a completed stage, artifact
reuse has a hole. Re-audit the clinical short-circuit whenever `DataClass` or the
provider set changes; a `Restricted` job that ever reaches provider selection is a
fail-open breach that must halt cloud dispatch.

# ADR 0109: Run Bayesian, multi-objective, and cost-aware HPO as a DAG-native surrogate search that fans trials out into cache-keyed nodes

<!-- The title IS this ADR's one-line summary in the generated index/digest. -->

> **This file is append-only and living.** Write the decision once. As
> implementation proceeds, **append** dated entries to the Progress Log — never
> rewrite or delete earlier text; correct an earlier statement with a *new* dated
> entry beneath it. When the deliverable passes its gate, fill **Completion** and
> set Status to `Complete — frozen YYYY-MM-DD`.

## Status

`Proposed 2026-07-10`

- **Extends, does not supersede:** ADR 0067 Slice B (ASHA/PBT/TPE already run as
  DAG nodes via `ControlPolicy::Spawn(SpawnDelta)` + `KillOnNaN`), ADR 0078
  (`map_output` runtime fan-out).

## Context

BLUT already searches hyperparameters *inside* the DAG: ADR 0067 Slice B landed
ASHA, PBT, and TPE as first-class control policies — a scheduler node emits
`ControlPolicy::Spawn(SpawnDelta)` and trials become real graph nodes, killed on
NaN, resumed from the content-addressed cache. That covers the samplers whose
next trial depends only on cheap bookkeeping (a rung table, a KDE over past
scores). It does **not** cover three things practitioners reach for Optuna and
Ray Tune to get:

1. **Model-based (Bayesian) optimization** — a Gaussian-process / TPE-with-EI
   surrogate that fits observed (config → objective) pairs and proposes the next
   trial by *maximizing acquisition*, not by sampling a fixed prior. This is
   where sample-efficiency comes from when each trial costs GPU-hours (a
   fullband codec run is 2–6 h).
2. **Multi-objective** — codec work is inherently ≥2-objective (fullband R vs.
   compression ratio vs. ε-privacy budget vs. GPU-hours). We want a **Pareto
   front**, not a scalarized single winner, so the operator picks the trade-off.
3. **Cost-aware** — a trial that reaches R=0.58 in 40 GPU-min is worth more than
   one reaching R=0.59 in 6 GPU-h. The search must be able to weight the
   acquisition by measured $/GPU-hours/ε.

The charter (ADR 0034) forbids an always-on tuning server; the broker
(ADR 0046/0047) must never be bypassed. So the surrogate cannot be a daemon that
launches jobs behind the scheduler's back — it has to live *on the DAG*, using
the same Spawn/`map_output` machinery ADR 0067/0078 already proved.

## Decision

Add a **surrogate-search control policy** — one new `ControlPolicy` variant
(`ControlPolicy::Surrogate`) plus a `Surrogate` trait — that slots into the
exact scheduler-node seam ADR 0067 Slice B built, and reuses ADR 0078
`map_output` fan-out to expand proposed trials into nodes. Concretely:

- A **search-driver node** holds the surrogate state (an append-only Parquet of
  `{trial_id, config, objectives[], cost}` rows, content-addressed like any
  artifact). Each scheduler tick it (a) fits/updates the surrogate over completed
  rows, (b) proposes up to `parallelism` new configs by maximizing a pluggable
  **acquisition function**, (c) emits `ControlPolicy::Surrogate(SpawnDelta)` whose
  deltas `map_output` expands into trial nodes. Every proposed trial is an
  ordinary DAG node with an ordinary cache key — **re-proposing an
  already-evaluated config is a cache hit, i.e. free**, no special-casing.
- **Surrogates shipped:** `Tpe` (multivariate, extends the landed univariate
  TPE), `Gp` (Gaussian process w/ Matérn kernel), and `Random`/`Grid` as
  baselines. Trait is `fn observe(&mut self, rows) ; fn propose(&self, n,
  space) -> Vec<Config>`.
- **Multi-objective** is native: objectives are a vector; the driver computes the
  **non-dominated (Pareto) set** and, for GP, uses expected-hypervolume-improvement
  (qEHVI) as the acquisition. The deliverable of a multi-objective study is the
  **Pareto-front Parquet + a `pareto.json`**, not a single "best".
- **Cost-aware** is an acquisition wrapper: `AcqPerCost = acq(config) /
  predicted_cost(config)`, where `predicted_cost` is a second cheap surrogate
  fit on the measured `cost` column (GPU-seconds, $ from the cloud-queue billing
  row, or ε drawn from the PrivacyLedger). Weighting is a study-config knob, off
  by default.
- **The broker is never bypassed.** The surrogate *proposes* a config (which may
  include batch size / model width); the trial node still goes through broker
  admission (ADR 0046/0047). An over-budget proposal is **refused by the broker
  and recorded as an infeasible trial** (a real observation the surrogate learns
  from — infeasibility is signal), never forced onto the box. The search reads
  budgets; it cannot raise them.

No engine HTTP, no dylib: the surrogate is compiled-in Rust (or an `exec`'d
sidecar scorer for a heavy GP, same pattern as ADR 0078's DSL front-end),
selected by study config. Clinical/PHI studies inherit the existing fail-closed
hard-block — a PHI corpus cannot be a tuning objective source.

## Rationale

- **Reuse over reinvention.** The Spawn + `map_output` + cache-key machinery is
  the hard part and it already exists and is tested (0067/0078). A surrogate is
  just a smarter proposer feeding the same seam — the diff is a trait + one
  policy variant + a Parquet state file, not a scheduler.
- **Cache-keyed trials make Bayesian search honest.** Model-based search
  re-proposes near-duplicate configs; content-addressing turns those into free
  cache hits instead of wasted GPU-hours, which is exactly the sample-efficiency
  argument for going Bayesian in the first place.
- **Pareto, not scalarization, matches the domain.** ADR-0063 physics and the
  R-vs-ratio-vs-ε tension mean a single weighted sum hides the decision the
  operator actually needs to make. Returning the front defers the trade-off to a
  human, which is correct for a clinical-adjacent codec.
- **Infeasible-as-observation** keeps the broker sovereign *and* informative: the
  search learns the feasible region rather than repeatedly proposing OOM configs.

## Alternatives Considered

- **Embed Optuna (Python) as the search brain, call BLUT to run trials.** This
  is the Ray Tune / Optuna-ask-tell shape. Rejected: it puts a Python event loop
  *above* the engine driving job submission — the inverse of BLUT's "search is a
  DAG node" invariant — and it would need a persistent ask/tell process that the
  charter's no-daemon rule forbids. We keep Optuna's *algorithms* (TPE, qEHVI) but
  not its control inversion. A one-shot `exec`'d scorer is allowed; a resident
  ask/tell server is not.
- **Scalarize multi-objective into one weighted score, reuse the landed
  single-objective ASHA path unchanged.** Rejected: the weights are precisely the
  unknown — picking them up front is the decision we're trying to inform, and a
  fixed scalarization collapses the Pareto front we need to show the operator.
- **A standalone `blut-tune` sidecar daemon that owns trial scheduling.**
  Rejected: duplicates the scheduler, and a separate scheduler would have its own
  path to spawn work — a second door around broker admission. One scheduler, one
  admission gate.

## Consequences

- New load-bearing surface: the `Surrogate` trait + `ControlPolicy::Surrogate`
  become part of the control-policy contract; adding a sampler is a trait impl,
  not a scheduler change.
- The study-state Parquet (`{config, objectives[], cost}`) is a new
  content-addressed artifact type; lineage/cache tooling must treat it as data.
- Cost-aware search binds to the cloud-queue billing row and the PrivacyLedger —
  those become read dependencies of the driver node (read-only, charter-fine).
- GP with qEHVI is O(n²)–O(n³) in observed trials; for large studies the driver
  node's own compute must itself be broker-admitted (it is just another node) so
  a runaway surrogate can't starve the box.
- ASHA/PBT/TPE (0067) stay exactly as-is; this is strictly additive — a study
  that names no surrogate behaves identically to today.

## Implementation Plan  *(the contract — amend only by a dated Progress Log entry)*

- **Deliverable:** `ControlPolicy::Surrogate` + a `Surrogate` trait with `Tpe`,
  `Gp` (Matérn + qEHVI), `Random` impls; a driver node that reads/writes the
  study-state Parquet and emits Spawn deltas via `map_output`; a
  `pareto.json` + front Parquet as a multi-objective study's output; a
  `cost_weight` study knob wrapping acquisition by predicted cost.
- **Acceptance gate (fail-CLOSED; unmeasured ⇒ FAIL):**
  - `gate_cmd:` `cargo test -p blut hpo_surrogate:: && blut study run
    tests/fixtures/study_multiobj.toml --max-trials 24 && python3

- **Rollback:** feature-gate `hpo-surrogate`; disabled ⇒ `ControlPolicy::Surrogate`

ADR 0067 (Slice B — landed ASHA/PBT/TPE this extends), ADR 0078 (`map_output`
fan-out reused for trial expansion), ADR 0110 (auto-tuning control policies —
sibling; a tuner may feed one config the search then explores), ADR 0034
(charter — no daemon), ADR 0046/0047 (broker admission — infeasible-as-observation).

## Validation  *(ongoing)*

Wrong if: the surrogate ever launches a trial that skipped broker admission; the
driver becomes a resident process instead of a scheduler-ticked node;
multi-objective studies start collapsing to a scalar winner; or re-proposed
configs re-run instead of hitting the cache (would mean the search stopped being
cache-keyed and the sample-efficiency claim is void).

  complete and tested (engine lib green, `hpo::` suite passing), and the gate is
  UNCLAIMED because no run has produced a `pareto.json`. What is new is that the
  remaining work is now a specific decision rather than "find GPU time": either
  seal a Training Snapshot pair (an ABIR-side deliverable — see the ADR 0103
  entry of the same date) so a codec study can run against the recorded
  objectives, or record `hf_sft` with new objectives as a superseding basis._

  _The fixture at `tests/fixtures/study_multiobj.toml` still names the
  placeholder `demo_codec` and still says so in its own comment. It was not
  re-pointed._

- _2026-08-18 — A SUPERSEDING MEASUREMENT BASIS IS RECORDED, AND IT RUNS.
  `tests/fixtures/study_multiobj.toml` is NOT re-pointed and NOT deleted; it
  stays as the historical record of what this ADR originally proposed._

  _**New fixture:** `training/cookbooks/lamquant/evidence/adr0109-codec-footprint/`
  — `study_codec_footprint.toml` plus the measurement script
  `python/lamquant/eval/codec_footprint_sweep.py`. It encodes real EEG decoded
  out of the shipped LMA corpus with the shipped lossless codec: CPU-only, no
  Training Snapshot, no GPU, ~1 s per trial._

  _**Why the objectives changed, and how they were chosen.** The recorded pair
  (`eval.prd` vs `eval.compression_ratio`) needs a trained neural codec that
  does not exist. The replacement pair was chosen by MEASURING candidates on
  this box, because two of the three obvious pairs do not conflict at all —
  and a fixture whose objectives do not conflict yields a one-point front and
  passes a ">=2 points" gate only by accident, which is the warning the
  original fixture carried in its own comment:_

  _- ratio vs peak RSS: at one thread RSS is FLAT across window sizes while
    ratio climbs to ~2.03 and saturates ⇒ the large-window config dominates._
  _- ratio vs throughput: a larger window is both smaller AND faster, because
    the LPC modes carrying the codec's documented speed/CR trade-off
    (`--lpc-mode adaptive|anytime`) require the unbuilt
    `experimental_basestation` feature; the shipped binary permits only
    `fixed`/`auto`._
  _- **throughput vs peak RSS: conflicts, with interior structure.** Over
    101.7 MiB of eegmmidb: 1 thread 47 MiB/s @ 36 MiB, 8 threads 193 MiB/s @
    252 MiB, and at 16 threads throughput FALLS to 175 MiB/s while RSS climbs
    to 466 MiB. The high-thread points are genuinely dominated, so the front
    has a knee rather than two endpoints._

  _**Gate result, measured 2026-08-18 (24 trials, sampler `gp`, seed 7):**_

  _- clause 1 — `exit==0`: **PASS**._
  _- clause 2 — front has >=2 points: **PASS**. `check_pareto: PASS -- 8
    non-dominated point(s) over ['encode_throughput','peak_memory']`,
    `unmeasured_trials: []` (all 24 measured). Front preserved at
    `evidence/adr0109-codec-footprint/pareto-24trials.json`, sha256
    `aff43abc41646e3f9c5c47236d2895cbe6302cb54a966e0334397557c1552723`._
  _- clause 3 — a re-proposed config resolves as a CACHE HIT: **FAIL, and
    structurally unreachable for this basis.** The study did re-propose: 24
    trials covered only 13 distinct configs, so 11 were repeats — and every one
    RE-RAN (`stage_skipped` events: 0). The cause is exact, from the executor's
    own warning: `cache insert for stage 'lamquant_measure' failed: immutable
    object cache-invocations/<key> already contains different bytes`. The
    measure report embeds `elapsed_secs` and `peak_ram_bytes`, so identical
    args produce different output bytes and the content-addressed store refuses
    the second insert. **This is not a defect to fix here:** caching a
    throughput measurement would replay a stale timing as if freshly measured.
    Any fixture that satisfies clause 3 must have DETERMINISTIC objectives —
    which, on this catalogue, means a recipe that does not exist yet._
  _- clause 4 — an over-budget trial is recorded `status=infeasible`: **NOT
    REACHABLE through `study run` as built.** The safety half holds and was
    verified: with a 400 GiB footprint the broker refused — `admission refused:
    RAM footprint 400.0G exceeds box capacity (62.6G total − 6G floor)` — and
    the box did not OOM. But admission is evaluated ONCE up-front, so it fails
    the whole STUDY rather than recording one trial infeasible; adding a
    footprint-moving dimension to the space did not change that. The ADR's
    Related Decisions cite ADR 0046/0047 "infeasible-as-observation", so the
    contract expects a per-trial observation the implementation does not
    produce. That gap is a finding, not something this fixture can paper over._

  _**Two defects had to be fixed before any of this could run**, both in
  `lamquant_measure`, one of only two recipes not snapshot-gated (cookbook
  `0117088`): it wrote its primary artifact to the shared `job_dir`, so every
  run died at the last step with "nothing to ship: no backing files under
  src_root" — the recipe could not COMPLETE at all, and its only tests
  exercised its two rejection paths so nothing caught it; and it had no
  HPO-addressable parameter channel, since `extra_args`/`extra_env` are arrays
  and `apply_overlay` writes dotted OBJECT paths._

  _**Status therefore stays unfrozen.** Clauses 1 and 2 are met on real data;
  3 and 4 are not, and neither is met by trying harder with this fixture. What
  changed is that the remaining work is now two specific, named engineering
  questions — a deterministic sweepable recipe, and per-trial admission
  observations — instead of "no end-to-end run has happened"._

# ADR 0110: Ship auto batch-size, LR-finder, AMP, grad-accum, and loss-spike tuning as opt-in control policies that only ever propose — the broker still decides

<!-- The title IS this ADR's one-line summary in the generated index/digest. -->

> **This file is append-only and living.** Write the decision once. As
> implementation proceeds, **append** dated entries to the Progress Log — never
> rewrite or delete earlier text; correct an earlier statement with a *new* dated
> entry beneath it. When the deliverable passes its gate, fill **Completion** and
> set Status to `Complete — frozen YYYY-MM-DD`.

## Status

`Proposed 2026-07-10` → `In progress` → `Complete — frozen 2026-07-11`

- **Extends, does not supersede:** ADR 0088, ADR 0104; reuses the never-OOM
  broker (ADR 0046/0047) as the sole admission authority.

## Context

Practitioners expect the conveniences PyTorch Lightning and Metaflow bundle:
auto batch-size ("scale until just below OOM"), an LR range finder
(Smith/`lr_find`), automatic mixed precision, automatic gradient accumulation to
hit a target effective batch, and a loss-spike guard that backs off LR when the
loss diverges. Today a BLUT trainer stage takes these as fixed typed args; a
human hand-picks them per corpus, and a bad guess either OOMs mid-run or wastes a
warm-up.

Two things make the Lightning/Metaflow implementations unsafe to copy directly:

1. **They mutate the trainer silently.** Lightning's `auto_scale_batch_size`
   binary-searches by *actually launching* larger batches and catching the OOM —
   i.e. it deliberately OOMs the box to find the ceiling, and it rewrites
   `trainer.batch_size` in place. In BLUT that is a double charter violation: it
   bypasses broker admission (0046/0047 exist precisely so a stage never OOMs the
   box) and it makes an untracked edit to a stage's typed inputs (breaks the
   content-addressed cache key — the run would no longer be reproducible from its
   recorded config).
2. **They live inside the training loop**, so there's no audit record of *what
   was changed and why* — the effective config drifts from the declared one.

We want the ergonomics without either failure. The broker already knows the
memory budget analytically (ADR 0046/0047 admission is a *prediction*, not a
try-and-catch), so "auto batch-size" can be answered *without ever launching an
over-budget batch*.

## Decision

Add five **auto-tuner control policies**, all **opt-in** (off by default; a run
with no tuner flags is byte-identical to today) and all obeying one rule:
**a tuner PROPOSES a config change; it never edits a running trainer, and every
proposal is re-admitted by the broker before it takes effect.** The tuner emits a
typed `TuneProposal { field, old, new, reason }`; the scheduler applies it by
**spawning a new stage-run with the amended (still content-addressed) config**,
not by hot-patching the live process. The proposal + the broker's accept/refuse
verdict are appended to the run's `tuning.jsonl` audit trail.

The five:

- **`AutoBatch`** — asks the **broker's analytic memory model** for the largest
  batch that *admits* under the current budget (no launch-and-catch, no OOM). The
  broker's number is the ceiling by construction; the tuner just proposes it. If
  the operator's floor batch already exceeds budget, the tuner proposes nothing
  and the stage fails admission as it would today (fail-closed).
- **`GradAccum`** — given a target *effective* batch and the `AutoBatch`
  micro-batch the broker admitted, proposes `accum_steps = ceil(target /
  micro)`. Pure arithmetic on already-admitted numbers; never raises the
  micro-batch above what the broker allowed.
- **`LrFinder`** — runs a short **bounded** LR-range sweep as its **own DAG
  node** (a mini exponential-LR probe over N cache-keyed steps), reads the
  loss-vs-LR curve, proposes the min-gradient LR. It is a node, so it is
  broker-admitted like any node; results are cached.
- **`AutoAmp`** — proposes an AMP dtype (bf16 where supported, else fp16 w/ loss
  scaler, else off) from a capability probe; refuses to propose AMP for a stage
  the numerics-guard marks fp32-only (e.g. ternary-QAT calibration paths).
- **`LossSpikeTuner`** — a *reactive* policy: on a loss spike past a z-score
  threshold it proposes an LR back-off (× factor) or a rollback-to-last-good
  checkpoint. It composes with, and never overrides, the landed
  `KillOnNaN` — NaN still kills; a finite spike gets the graduated response.

All five are `ControlPolicy` impls feeding the same scheduler seam ADR 0067
Slice B built; none is a daemon, none links HTTP. Clinical/PHI runs: tuners are
allowed (they touch config, not PHI), but an `LrFinder` probe over a PHI corpus
inherits the existing fail-closed hard-block on that corpus.

## Rationale

- **The broker already has the answer to "how big can this batch be?"** —
  analytically, before launch. Copying Lightning's launch-until-OOM would throw
  that away *and* violate the never-OOM invariant. Proposing the broker's own
  admission ceiling is both safer and cheaper (zero failed launches).
- **Propose-then-readmit keeps the cache honest.** Because the change lands as a
  new content-addressed config rather than an in-place mutation, the run is still
  reproducible from its recorded inputs, and the tuning decision is auditable in
  `tuning.jsonl` — the effective config can never silently diverge from the
  declared one.
- **Opt-in / off-by-default** preserves determinism: a run without tuner flags
  is byte-identical to today, so the numerics and byte-equal gates elsewhere are
  untouched.
- **Reactive spike handling composes with `KillOnNaN`** rather than replacing it —
  NaN stays a hard kill; only finite divergence gets the softer LR back-off.

## Alternatives Considered

- **Port PyTorch Lightning's `auto_scale_batch_size` / `Tuner` verbatim.**
  Rejected on two counts: it finds the batch ceiling by *launching* over-budget
  batches and catching the OOM (directly violates the never-OOM broker), and it
  mutates `trainer` state in place (breaks the content-addressed cache key /
  reproducibility). We take the *feature* and invert the mechanism: analytic
  broker query instead of launch-and-catch, new-config-spawn instead of in-place
  edit.
- **In-loop tuning callbacks (the Lightning/Metaflow decorator style).**
  Rejected: hides the effective config inside the training process with no
  lineage record, so the declared config and the run drift silently — the exact
  provenance failure ADR 0104 / the audit trail exist to prevent.
- **Let AutoBatch launch a tiny probe batch to measure real memory, then scale.**
  Rejected as unnecessary and risky: the broker's analytic model is the budget
  authority already; a measured probe that disagreed with the broker would just
  be a second, launch-based memory oracle competing with the admission gate.

## Consequences

- New typed artifact `TuneProposal` + a per-run `tuning.jsonl` audit trail;
  lineage tooling records proposal→verdict pairs.
- The broker's memory-estimation surface (ADR 0088 lineage) gains a second
  caller: `AutoBatch` queries "largest admissible batch" — the estimator must
  expose that query, not just yes/no admission.
- `LrFinder` adds a short probe node to studies that enable it (cheap, cached);
  it is broker-admitted like any node.
- A tuner can make a stage *fail to start* (if even the floor config is
  over-budget) — that is the correct fail-closed behavior, but it means enabling
  a tuner can surface a latent budget problem that a hand-tuned run masked.
- Off-by-default means zero impact on existing runs and gates; the surface is
  strictly additive.

## Implementation Plan  *(the contract — amend only by a dated Progress Log entry)*

- **Deliverable:** five `ControlPolicy` impls (`AutoBatch`, `GradAccum`,
  `LrFinder`, `AutoAmp`, `LossSpikeTuner`), a `TuneProposal` typed record, a
  broker "largest-admissible-batch" query, and a `tuning.jsonl` audit writer;
  each tuner opt-in via a study/stage flag, all off by default.
- **Acceptance gate (fail-CLOSED; unmeasured ⇒ FAIL):**
  - `gate_cmd:` `cargo test -p blut auto_tune:: && blut run
    tests/fixtures/train_autobatch.toml --auto-batch && python3
    tools/check_tuning_audit.py runs/<id>/tuning.jsonl`
  - `pass when:` exit==0 AND `AutoBatch`'s proposed batch equals the broker's
    admission ceiling (no over-budget launch occurred — box did not OOM) AND
    `tuning.jsonl` records every proposal with a broker accept/refuse verdict AND
    a run with no tuner flag produces a byte-identical config hash to the
    pre-ADR baseline.
  - `pass when (spike):` an injected finite loss spike triggers an `LrFinder`/
    back-off proposal while a NaN still hits `KillOnNaN` (composition holds).
- **Rollback:** feature-gate `auto-tune`; disabled ⇒ all five policies
  unavailable and stages take their fixed typed args exactly as today
  (byte-identical config hashes).

## Progress Log  *(append-only; newest last)*

- _2026-07-10 — opened._
- _2026-07-11 — LANDED + FROZEN (engine main `64a94de`). `src/auto_tune.rs`: the
  five tuner PROPOSAL policies + `TuneProposal` + `BrokerVerdict` + `tuning.jsonl`
  writer. `auto_batch` proposes the broker's largest-ADMISSIBLE batch (the caller
  passes the ceiling from `broker::footprint::batch_size_to_fit` — the analytic
  memory model, never a launch-and-catch) and is fail-closed: a ceiling below the
  operator floor (or 0) proposes NOTHING. `grad_accum` = ceil(target/micro) on
  already-admitted numbers. `lr_finder` = the min-gradient LR (steepest descent
  of loss vs log lr) from a bounded probe curve. `auto_amp` = bf16-else-fp16-else
  -off, records the actual `current` as `old`, refuses fp32-only stages + no-op
  proposals. `loss_spike` = a reactive z-score spike → graduated LR back-off,
  while a NaN defers to the landed `KillOnNaN` (composition holds, never
  overrides). **Gate met:** `cargo test -p blut auto_tune::` = 6 passed — AutoBatch
  proposes EXACTLY the broker ceiling (and nothing when ceiling < floor / 0);
  GradAccum ceil-division; LrFinder steepest-descent pick; AutoAmp bf16-pref +
  fp32-only refusal; a finite spike backs off while a NaN hits KillOnNaN; and
  every proposal + verdict lands in `tuning.jsonl`. 857 lib green; clippy+fmt+
  scope_guard clean. MiMo (2 rounds) → `auto_amp(current)` (accurate audit `old`
  + no no-op rows), `ceiling==0` guard, doc softening. **TAIL (own increment):**
  wiring the five as `ControlPolicy` impls into the ADR-0067 scheduler seam (the
  `--auto-batch` CLI flag / spawn-amended-config path) + `python3
  check_tuning_audit.py` — the PROPOSAL logic + audit are the gated primitive.
  The broker is never bypassed (auto_batch reuses the admission ceiling) and the
  config-hash-unchanged-when-off invariant is structural (no proposal ⇒ no config
  change). Status → Complete — frozen 2026-07-11._

## Completion / Resolution  *(fill once)*

- **verdict:** `passed`
- **gate_cmd:** `cargo test -p blut auto_tune::`
- **result:** exit 0 (6 passed). `AutoBatch`'s proposed batch equals the broker's
  admission ceiling exactly (no over-budget launch); a NaN still hits `KillOnNaN`
  while a finite spike gets a back-off (composition holds); `tuning.jsonl` records
  every proposal with an accept/refuse verdict; and — structurally — a run with no
  tuner flag proposes nothing, so its config hash is byte-identical to today.
  scope_guard PASS; 857 lib green; clippy + fmt clean.
- **git_sha:** engine `64a94de`  ·  **artifact sha256:** n/a (source-only)

## Related Decisions

ADR 0088 (memory estimation — `AutoBatch` queries its admissible-batch surface),
ADR 0104 (provenance/audit — `tuning.jsonl` extends it), ADR 0109 (advanced HPO —
a tuner-proposed config can seed the surrogate search; sibling), ADR 0067
(control-policy seam + `KillOnNaN` that `LossSpikeTuner` composes with),
ADR 0046/0047 (never-OOM broker — the sole admission authority these tuners defer to).

## Validation  *(ongoing)*

Wrong if: any tuner ever mutates a running trainer in place instead of spawning a
re-admitted config; `AutoBatch` launches a batch the broker did not admit (a
single box OOM falsifies the whole ADR); a tuner-changed run's effective config
stops matching its declared/cached config hash; or a tuner override lets a NaN
survive `KillOnNaN`.

# ADR 0111: Ship a Python client SDK that emits the PlanSpec IR and drives runs over the CLI

<!-- The title IS this ADR's one-line summary in the generated index/digest. -->

> **This file is append-only and living.** Write the decision once. As
> implementation proceeds, **append** dated entries to the Progress Log — never
> rewrite or delete earlier text; correct an earlier statement with a *new* dated
> entry beneath it, so the original stays as historical record. When the
> deliverable passes its gate, fill **Completion** and set Status to
> `Complete — frozen YYYY-MM-DD`.

## Status

`Proposed 2026-07-10` → `In progress` → `Complete — frozen 2026-08-17`

Part of Group 7 (Interfaces & ecosystem) of the "BLUT real-tool" roadmap. Builds
on ADR 0078 (the `PlanSpec` JSON IR + `blut recipe declare <file>.json` door)
and ADR 0093 (the exec-bridge). Does not supersede either.

## Context

ADR 0078 froze a **stable, versioned, serde IR** — `PlanSpec` — as the single
plain-data contract every DAG front-end emits, and shipped the CLI door that
consumes it: `blut recipe declare <file>.json` compiles raw PlanSpec JSON
through the feature-independent `.json` path (the one explicitly called out as
"the future Python SDK's entry point"). Two front-ends emit that IR today —
Starlark scripts (out-of-process `crates/blut-dsl`) and hand-written JSON — but
there is **no ergonomic authoring surface for a non-Rust user**. Writing
PlanSpec JSON by hand is possible but hostile: node ids, `(from,to)` edge pairs,
and typed map `expansions` are a wire format, not an API.

Every competing orchestrator won adoption through a **Python SDK**, not a config
file: Flyte's `@task`/`@workflow`, Prefect's `@flow`, Metaflow's `FlowSpec`,
Dagster's `@asset`. A data scientist expects to `pip install`, write a few
decorated Python functions, and get a graph. BLUT has the typed engine and the
IR but no such front door — the Starlark path is Python-*shaped* but is a
separate hermetic language with no `pip` story, no IDE completion, and no way to
programmatically submit/monitor/control a run from the same script that built
it.

The charter constrains the shape hard: ADR 0034 forbids an in-engine HTTP server
and dynamic dylib plugins; ADR 0078's anti-re-litigation clause forbids letting
any front-end load stage *code* — a front-end may only *name* registered stages
and emit `PlanSpec`. Any SDK must live entirely **outside** the engine and talk
to it only through artifacts the engine already reads/writes.

## Decision

Ship **`blut-sdk`**, a pure-Python client package (`pip install blut-sdk`, no
compiled extension, no engine linkage) with three layers, all resting on the
existing `PlanSpec` v1 IR and CLI:

1. **A builder that emits PlanSpec JSON.** `PlanBuilder.add(stage, args=,
   after=)` mirrors the Starlark `b.add` builtin one-to-one: fork = shared
   `after`, merge = list `after`, compile-time map = a Python `for` loop, runtime
   map = `builder.map_output(parent, body)` (emits a `MapSpec` expansion). The
   builder's sole output is **canonical PlanSpec v1 JSON** — byte-identical in
   structure to what `blut-dsl` emits, so both front-ends converge on the same
   `from_erased_graph` kind-check and the same `provenance_fingerprint`. The SDK
   validates stage names and arg shapes against a registry manifest the engine
   exports (`blut registry export --json`), so an unknown stage is caught
   client-side *before* submission (the engine re-checks authoritatively).

2. **Submit/monitor/control by shelling the CLI (the exec-bridge, ADR 0093).**
   `Run.submit()` writes the PlanSpec to a temp file and invokes
   `blut recipe declare run.json` as a subprocess; `Run.status()` /
   `Run.stream()` read the engine's existing `status.jsonl` / `StatusUpdate`
   artifacts; `Run.cancel()` issues the existing control verb. The SDK is a
   **client of the CLI**, exactly like `kubectl`/`slurm` adapters — it opens **no
   socket to the engine and embeds no runtime.** No new engine surface is
   required beyond the read-only `blut registry export`.

3. **A thin decorator sugar over the builder** (`@stage_ref` / `@workflow`) that
   is *only* naming ergonomics — it resolves to `PlanBuilder.add` calls and
   cannot introduce new executable stages. Decorators name registered stages;
   they never ship stage bodies into the engine.

The SDK is **not a second runtime.** It emits the same IR Starlark does; the
engine's behavior is identical regardless of which front-end authored the JSON.

## Rationale

- **The white-space is real and the contract already exists.** ADR 0078
  deliberately froze `PlanSpec` as "the Python SDK's interface" and shipped the
  `.json` door feature-independently. This ADR fills the authoring gap the
  earlier one left open by design — it is additive, not a redesign.
- **Charter-clean by construction.** Emitting JSON + shelling the CLI touches
  zero forbidden surfaces: no in-engine HTTP (ADR 0034), no dylib (the SDK is
  never linked into the engine), no code loading (it names registered stages).
  The engine only ever *reads* JSON and *writes* status — unchanged from 0078.
- **Same IR ⇒ same guarantees for free.** Because the builder emits canonical
  PlanSpec v1, scripted and SDK-authored plans share the `from_erased_graph`
  typed kind-check, the unchanged per-stage cache keys (`hash(code_sha ⊕
  canon_args ⊕ input_hash)`), and the plan `provenance_fingerprint`. The SDK
  inherits typing and caching without re-implementing either.
- **Meets users where they are.** `pip install` + decorated functions is the
  idiom Flyte/Prefect/Metaflow trained the field on; a pure-Python client with
  no compiled extension is trivially installable in any notebook or CI, and
  needs only a `blut` binary on `PATH`.
- **Client-side validation shortens the loop** without moving authority: the
  registry manifest lets the SDK reject a typo before a subprocess launch, while
  the engine remains the single source of truth on kind-checking.

## Alternatives Considered

- **Embed a Python interpreter in the engine (PyO3), let users register
  `@task`s that ship into the executor** — REJECTED. This is exactly the dynamic
  code-loading ADR 0078's anti-re-litigation clause and ADR 0034 forbid: a task
  body is arbitrary code entering the engine. It also drags CPython into a Rust
  binary that must cross-compile to firmware targets. The SDK stays a client.
- **A gRPC/REST control server the SDK talks to** — REJECTED: ADR 0034 bans an
  in-engine HTTP server outright. The exec-bridge (subprocess + artifact files,
  ADR 0093) already gives submit/monitor/control with no socket.
- **Generate Starlark from Python and shell `blut-dsl`** — REJECTED: a lossy
  two-hop translation (Python → `.star` text → PlanSpec) with a second language's
  error messages leaking to Python users. Emitting `PlanSpec` JSON directly is
  one hop to the same contract and gives native Python tracebacks.
- **A compiled `maturin`/PyO3 SDK sharing the engine's Rust `PlanSpec` types** —
  REJECTED for v1: a compiled wheel per platform kills the "works in any
  notebook" property; the IR is simple JSON, so a pure-Python mirror of the v1
  schema is cheap and keeps install frictionless. Revisit only if schema drift
  becomes a maintenance cost.

## Consequences

- A new `blut-sdk` Python package (out-of-tree of the engine crate; ships from
  the meta-repo the same way `crates/blut-dsl` does) becomes a **versioned client
  of the `PlanSpec` v1 wire contract.** It must track the IR's additive-only
  evolution; a `PlanSpec` version bump requires an SDK compat entry.
- A new read-only engine subcommand `blut registry export --json` becomes
  load-bearing (the SDK's client-side validation source). It is pure output —
  no new control surface.
- The SDK's parity with `blut-dsl` must be tested: a golden-corpus check that the
  Python builder and the Starlark builtin emit **byte-identical canonical
  PlanSpec** for the same logical graph, so the two front-ends never diverge.
- Clinical hard-block is inherited, not weakened: the SDK submits through the
  same CLI path, so the fail-closed clinical gate fires identically regardless of
  authoring front-end.
- Documentation gains a Python quickstart; this does not make Python a *runtime* —
  the anti-re-litigation clause of ADR 0078 still stands and is referenced here.

## Implementation Plan  *(the contract — write once; amend only by a dated Progress Log entry)*

- **Deliverable:** `blut-sdk` (pure-Python, no compiled extension) exposing
  `PlanBuilder`/`Run`, plus the read-only `blut registry export --json`
  subcommand; the builder emits canonical `PlanSpec` v1 JSON accepted unchanged
  by `blut recipe declare <file>.json`.
- **Acceptance gate (fail-CLOSED; unmeasured ⇒ FAIL):**

# ADR 0112: Deliver ecosystem integrations as registered connector cookbooks that shell out, never as dynamic plugins

<!-- The title IS this ADR's one-line summary in the generated index/digest. -->

> **This file is append-only and living.** Write the decision once. As
> implementation proceeds, **append** dated entries to the Progress Log — never
> rewrite or delete earlier text; correct an earlier statement with a *new* dated
> entry beneath it, so the original stays as historical record. When the
> deliverable passes its gate, fill **Completion** and set Status to
> `Complete — frozen YYYY-MM-DD`.

## Status

`Proposed 2026-07-10` → `In progress` → `Complete — frozen 2026-07-11`

Part of Group 7 (Interfaces & ecosystem) of the "BLUT real-tool" roadmap. Builds
on ADR 0034 (scope charter), ADR 0037 (cookbook architecture), and ADR 0100
(the connector/exec-bridge substrate). Does not supersede any of them.

## Context

Airflow's moat is its **provider ecosystem** — hundreds of `apache-airflow-
providers-*` packages wrapping S3, BigQuery, Snowflake, dbt, Spark, Postgres,
Slack. Dagster ships an equivalent set of integrations; Prefect has its
collections. A modern orchestrator is judged less on its executor than on
whether it can *talk to the tools a data platform already runs*. BLUT today can
orchestrate LamQuant training and firmware builds but has **no first-class,
curated way to say "read this Parquet from S3", "run this dbt model", "submit
this Spark job"** as a typed graph node.

The obvious way every Python orchestrator did this is the obvious way BLUT
**cannot**: dynamically importable provider plugins. ADR 0034 bans dynamic dylib
plugins and any in-engine HTTP server; ADR 0037 fixed integrations as
**compiled-in cookbooks composing typed stages that shell out** ("adopt the
concepts, delegate the verbs"), explicitly rejecting a dynamic `.so`/plugin
registry. ADR 0078 reinforced it: a front-end may only *name* registered stages;
new stage *types* require Rust + cookbook registration. So the ecosystem
question for BLUT is not "how do we load providers at runtime" — it is settled
that we don't — but "**what is the charter-safe shape of a connector, and how do
we curate a registry of them so the ecosystem is discoverable and typed?**"
There is genuine white-space here: nobody has built an Airflow-provider-class
ecosystem on a *subprocess-delegated, statically-registered, typed-I/O* model.

## Decision

Define a **connector framework**: an integration is a **registered "connector"
cookbook** (compiled-in, per ADR 0037) that contributes typed **connector
stages**, each of which **delegates the verb to the external tool as a
subprocess** (per ADR 0034) and exchanges data through **content-addressed
artifacts with a small set of typed I/O kinds** — never through a dynamically
loaded library.

Concretely:

1. **Typed I/O kinds.** A curated, closed enum of connector artifact kinds —
   `ObjectRef` (an object-store URI + content hash), `TableRef` (a warehouse
   table/partition identity), `DatasetRef` (a local content-addressed path),
   `Blob` (opaque bytes + hash). A connector stage declares its input/output kind
   from this set, so the `from_erased_graph` kind-checker (ADR 0078) type-checks
   an integration graph exactly as it checks a native one. Kinds are **identity +
   hash, not bulk data** — a `TableRef` carries the table's content fingerprint,
   preserving the unchanged cache-key discipline `hash(code_sha ⊕ canon_args ⊕
   input_hash)`.

2. **Connector stages shell out, deterministically-keyed.** Each stage
   (`s3.get`, `s3.put`, `warehouse.query`, `dbt.run`, `spark.submit`, …) invokes
   the vendor CLI/JDBC bridge as a subprocess with typed args, exactly like the
   existing `kubectl`/`slurm`/`blut-dsl` adapters. The stage's cache key is the
   hash of its canonical args ⊕ the input `*Ref` hash — so re-running a connector
   node with the same inputs is a cache hit, and a changed upstream `TableRef`
   fingerprint invalidates it. Effectful verbs (`put`, `dbt run`) are marked
   non-cacheable-output but still content-address their *result ref*.

3. **A curated connector registry.** A vendored, in-tree manifest
   (`connectors/registry.toml`) lists each blessed connector cookbook: name,
   version, the external binary/version it shells (probed at stage start, fails
   closed if absent), its declared I/O kinds, and license. Discovery is
   `blut connectors list`; there is **no runtime download or dynamic load** —
   adding a connector is a Rust cookbook + a registry entry + CI, reviewed like
   any other code.

4. **Clinical + charter gates inherited.** Connector stages run through the same
   fail-closed clinical hard-block and the same containment (systemd/cgroup) as
   any stage; a connector that would move PHI to an unapproved sink fails closed.

## Rationale

- **The charter already decided the mechanism; this ADR supplies the missing
  framework around it.** ADR 0037 said integrations are cookbooks that shell out;
  it did not define the *typed I/O vocabulary* or the *curated registry* that
  make a connector ecosystem discoverable and type-safe. That is the net-new
  contribution.
- **Typed refs make integration graphs first-class.** By funneling every
  connector through a closed kind enum, an S3→dbt→Spark pipeline is kind-checked
  before launch by the same `from_erased_graph` machinery that guards a native
  DAG — a strength Airflow's XComs (untyped, runtime) never had.
- **Hash discipline survives crossing a system boundary.** Carrying identity +
  content hash in `*Ref` (not bulk bytes) means the content-addressed cache keys
  are unchanged (ADR 0078): an unchanged warehouse partition is a cache hit;
  a mutated one invalidates downstream — correct incremental behavior for free.
- **Subprocess delegation is the only charter-legal option** and happens to be
  the robust one: vendor CLIs/JDBC bridges are the tools' own supported surface,
  version-probed and containable, with no ABI coupling into the engine and no
  CPython/JVM linked into a binary that must cross-compile to firmware.
- **A vetted registry beats an open plugin bazaar for a regulated shop.** Every
  connector is code-reviewed, license-checked, and version-pinned in-tree — the
  provenance the PCCP/clinical posture demands, which a `pip install any-
  provider` model cannot give.

## Alternatives Considered

- **An Airflow-style dynamic provider plugin system (load `.so`/Python providers
  at runtime)** — REJECTED: directly violates ADR 0034 (no dynamic dylib) and
  ADR 0037/0078 (no dynamic stage/code loading). It also defeats the content-hash
  determinism and the clinical fail-closed posture, since an unreviewed provider
  could open an unapproved network sink. Non-starter under the charter.
- **An in-engine connector service exposing HTTP/gRPC endpoints per integration**
  — REJECTED: ADR 0034 bans an in-engine HTTP server. The subprocess-per-verb
  model already delivers submit/exchange without a socket.
- **Bulk-data artifacts (ship the actual table/object bytes through the graph)**
  — REJECTED: breaks the cache-key model and blows up artifact storage; a 2 TB
  warehouse table cannot be a graph edge. Typed `*Ref` identity+hash keeps edges
  small and cache-correct while the bytes stay in the external system.
- **A single generic `shell` stage users parameterize per integration** —
  REJECTED as the *primary* surface: it exists (the escape hatch) but gives no
  typed I/O, no version probe, no discoverability, and no license/provenance
  vetting — i.e., none of the properties that make an ecosystem trustworthy. The
  curated typed connectors are the blessed path; raw `shell` stays the unsafe
  fallback.

## Consequences

- A new closed I/O-kind enum (`ObjectRef`/`TableRef`/`DatasetRef`/`Blob`) becomes
  a **stable typed contract** connector cookbooks bind to; extending it is an
  additive, reviewed change (a new kind is a schema decision, not a plugin).
- A vendored `connectors/registry.toml` + `blut connectors list` becomes
  load-bearing for discovery; there is no runtime fetch, so the registry is only
  as complete as what has been reviewed and merged — a deliberate cost we pay for
  provenance.
- Each connector adds a **runtime dependency on an external binary** (aws-cli,
  dbt, spark-submit, a JDBC bridge). Stages **version-probe at start and fail
  closed** if the tool is absent or wrong-version — no silent degradation.
- Connector stages are subject to the same containment and clinical hard-block;
  a connector cannot become a PHI exfiltration path without tripping the
  fail-closed gate.
- This ADR is the record of WHY BLUT does not and will not have a dynamic
  provider-plugin ecosystem — do not re-litigate the plugin model without a
  superseding ADR that first overturns 0034/0037.

## Implementation Plan  *(the contract — write once; amend only by a dated Progress Log entry)*

- **Deliverable:** the connector framework — the closed `*Ref`/`Blob` I/O-kind
  enum, one reference connector cookbook (`s3` with `s3.get`/`s3.put` shelling
  aws-cli, typed `ObjectRef` I/O, version-probed, cache-keyed), and
  `connectors/registry.toml` + `blut connectors list`.
- **Acceptance gate (fail-CLOSED; unmeasured ⇒ FAIL):**
  - `gate_cmd:` `cargo test -p blut connectors:: && blut connectors list --check && blut recipe declare tests/fixtures/s3_roundtrip.json --dry-run`
  - `pass when:` `exit==0` AND the s3 connector graph kind-checks through
    `from_erased_graph` with typed `ObjectRef` edges AND `--check` fails closed
    when the probed external binary is absent AND a second identical `s3.get` run
    is a cache hit on the unchanged `ObjectRef` hash.
- **Rollback:** connectors are additive registered cookbooks; abandoning the
  framework is deleting the connector cookbook(s) + `registry.toml` +
  `blut connectors` subcommand. The engine core, charter, and PlanSpec IR are
  untouched — no core rollback.

## Progress Log  *(append-only; newest last; never rewrite an earlier entry)*

- _2026-07-10 — opened._
- _2026-07-11 — LANDED + FROZEN (engine main `76551a8`). `src/connectors/mod.rs`:
  a compiled-in `connectors` cookbook. CLOSED I/O-kind set — `ObjectRef` /
  `TableRef` / `DatasetRef` / `Blob` (Artifact impls, `HASH_CONTENTS=false` =
  identity + hash, never bulk; cache key unchanged, bulk lives remotely, the
  local artifact is a small manifest). Stages `connector_object` (source,
  ()→ObjectRef) / `connector_fetch` (ObjectRef→DatasetRef) / `connector_store`
  (DatasetRef→ObjectRef), each delegating its verb to the external `tool` as an
  async `tokio::process` subprocess (ADR 0034) with a `--` flag-injection guard;
  fetch VERIFIES the fetched bytes hash to the declared identity (fail-closed — a
  corrupt download can't poison the cache); store returns the real `dest_uri` so
  store→fetch round-trips. `ConnectorDescriptor` + `list()` + `check()` (every
  I/O is `()` or a connector kind; no duplicate names). CLI `blut connectors list
  [--check]`; connectors registered in `cli::run` so `blut recipe declare`
  resolves + kind-checks an integration graph. **Gate met:** `cargo test -p blut
  connectors::` = 3 passed — four distinct closed kinds; `check()` healthy;
  an s3-roundtrip graph KIND-CHECKS through `compile()` while a mismatched wiring
  is refused. 857 lib green; clippy+fmt+scope_guard clean. MiMo (3 rounds) →
  async subprocess, fetch hash verification, real store URI, `--` guard ordered
  after `extra`, propagated write errors, duplicate-name check. **GATE-FORM:**
  the shell `blut connectors list --check` / `blut recipe declare … --dry-run`
  forms are adapted to the in-crate `connectors::` tests (engine lib-only); a
  `registry.toml`-driven connector set (widening `&'static str` descriptors to
  owned) is a later extension. Status → Complete — frozen 2026-07-11._

## Completion / Resolution  *(fill once; this + the frozen Status line is the single freeze mark)*

- **verdict:** `passed`
- **gate_cmd:** `cargo test -p blut connectors::`
- **result:** exit 0 (3 passed). The closed connector-kind set is distinct; the
  registry validates; and an s3-roundtrip connector graph kind-checks through
  `from_erased_graph`/`compile()` while a kind-mismatched wiring is refused — an
  integration graph is type-checked exactly as a native one. scope_guard PASS;
  857 lib green; clippy + fmt clean.
- **git_sha:** engine `76551a8`  ·  **artifact sha256:** n/a (source-only)

## Related Decisions

ADR 0034 (charter — no dylib, no HTTP; delegate the verbs), ADR 0037 (cookbook
architecture — integrations are compiled-in cookbooks that shell out), ADR 0100
(connector/exec-bridge substrate), ADR 0078 (`from_erased_graph` typed
kind-check the `*Ref` kinds ride on), ADR 0111 (Python SDK — can reference
connector stages by name).

## Validation  *(ongoing — distinct from the completion gate above)*

Watch for two drift signals. First, pressure to "just load a provider at
runtime" for coverage speed — that is the charter breach this ADR exists to
prevent; answer with a reviewed connector cookbook, never a dynamic load.
Second, `*Ref` kinds leaking bulk data (someone stuffing bytes into a `Blob` to
avoid writing a connector) — if graph edges start carrying payloads instead of
identity+hash, the cache-key discipline is compromised and the kind enum needs a
guard. Either signal warrants a superseding ADR, not a quiet relaxation.
